React 19 + TypeScript SPA (frontend/src/mystic_auth/, with the entry point and extension surface, namely main.tsx, App.tsx, sdk.ts, app_sdk.ts, in the sibling frontend/src/app/; see Using This Repository as a Template), built with Vite, styled with Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui (Radix primitives). Feature-organized to mirror the backend's domain split, with a PBAC-aware UI layer that mirrors the backend's permission vocabulary.

Module Purpose auth/ Login, signup, logout, logout-all, OAuth2, password reset (request/confirm), account verification (including resend), current-user session query, the auth-refresh interceptor, useSessionEventsStream.ts (SSE connection to GET /auth/session-events, invalidates the current-user/sessions queries in real time on a push event), useCooldown (shared resend/retry cooldown timer); each sub-feature is its own folder (Page/Form/mutation-hook/types); password_rules/ holds password-complexity validation (passwordRules.ts) and its checklist UI, shared by signup/reset/account settings authorization/ The PBAC layer: permissions.ts (frontend mirror of the backend Permission enum), authorizationService.ts (batch permission-check calls, policy/audit-log fetches), useAuthorization/useCan (useAuthorized is a same-hook alias for call sites that read more naturally as "is the caller authorized" than "can the caller"), and the gate components Authorized, IfCan, ProtectedRoute audit_log/ AuditLogPage.tsx: just the tab shell (Authorization decisions/Security events x My activity/All users). Everything specific to just one tab lives inside its own subfolder: authorization_log/ (MyAuthorizationLogSection.tsx, AllAuthorizationLogSection.tsx, AuthorizationFilterBar.tsx, authorizationLogColumns.tsx, authorizationLogQueries.ts, authorizationLogResourceTypes.ts) and security_log/ (MySecurityLogSection.tsx, AllSecurityLogSection.tsx, SecurityFilterBar.tsx, securityLogColumns.tsx, securityLogQueries.ts, securityLogEventTypes.ts, LoginTrendChart.tsx). What's genuinely identical for both tabs stays flat at audit_log/ instead of being duplicated into each: auditLogListConfig.ts (PAGE_SIZE/formatTimestamp/etc.) and auditLogPageResult.ts (X-Total-Count -> {rows,total} parsing, shared by both *LogQueries.ts files) dashboard/ DashboardPage.tsx: the landing page after login - data-fetching and dialog orchestration only. DashboardIdentityCard.tsx (plus DashboardStatItem.tsx, its one stat-cell subcomponent) and DashboardIdentityCardSkeleton.tsx own the identity-card banner's loaded/loading presentation respectively, split out of DashboardPage.tsx once that file passed this repo's own file-length guideline - see Testing Overview. The page composes cards owned by domain folders such as active_sessions/. OperationsShortcutsCard.tsx owns the dashboard's operational shortcuts. active_sessions/ ActiveSessionsCard.tsx (its own top-level folder, because more than one page renders it) plus its own useSessionsQuery/useRevokeSessionMutation/parseUserAgent/activeSessionsTable.tsx, backed by /auth/sessions, and usePreviousLoginQuery.ts (the most recent successful login, GET /audit/security-log/me), which the Dashboard card and the session-event stream both use passkeys/ The Passkeys tab shown inside Account Settings: PasskeysCard.tsx, AddPasskeyForm, PasskeysBulkToolbar, passkeysTable.tsx, PasskeyStepUpDialog, usePasskeyManagement (owns the server calls) and useStepUpReturnToast. See Passkeys. A domain folder like active_sessions/; the page that shows it stays in account_settings/ policies/ Policy CRUD UI for PBAC policies, plus PolicyStatsCard.tsx permissions/ PermissionsPage.tsx: read-only, browsable view of MysticAuth's built-in permission catalog (GET /authorization/permissions/catalog, see authorization/permissions_catalog.py). It is separate from policies/ because the built-in reference and policy composition answer different questions. Downstream applications own their custom action catalog and management UI. Search, filter, sort, and pagination run client-side against the small built-in catalog rate_limits/ RateLimitsPage.tsx: operational view of RateLimitDashboardService.list_active_limits (GET /rate-limits), filterable by scope (ip/account/email) via RateLimitsFilterBar.tsx, plus useResetRateLimitMutation (rateLimitsMutations.ts) for DELETE /rate-limits/{key:path} account_settings/ AccountSettingsPage.tsx (nav label/route: "Account Settings"): self-service rename and change/set password, via two independent forms/cards, plus own effective policies. Deliberately omits email/role/member-since/session-count, which dashboard/ already shows as read-only context. Also useUnsavedChangesWarning (its only consumer). The page only composes cards: the Passkeys tab lives in passkeys/ and the delete-account card in account_deletion/. account_deletion/ DeleteAccountCard.tsx and its useDeleteMyAccountMutation drive self-service account deletion (password re-confirm for password accounts, an emailed confirm link for OAuth-only accounts). ConfirmDeleteAccountPage.tsx is the public /confirm-delete landing page the emailed link opens, with ConfirmDeleteAccountButton and useConfirmDeleteMyAccountMutation. See Account Deletion and Purge users/ User management under PBAC policy checks (list, mutate, assign policies), plus UserStatsCard.tsx api/ Axios-based typed call functions per backend domain (auth_api, users_api, account_settings_api, policies_api, permissions_api, bulk_assignment_api, rate_limits_api, audit_api), plus axiosInstance.ts and apiError.ts. The policy query modules under policies/queries/ wrap these clients for TanStack Query mutations. store/ Zustand: authStore.ts (session/profile/permissions), themeStore.ts (light/dark), appearanceStore.ts (the signed-in user's picked brand color, backed by localStorage, see Appearance), languageStore.ts (translation language mode, see Translations Overview), fontSizeStore.ts (small/medium/large, persisted to localStorage, applied as a percentage of the browser's own root font size so it composes with the user's OS/browser text-size setting), routeLoadingStore.ts (in-flight lazy-route-chunk counter, drives ui/routing/RouteProgressBar.tsx), networkStatusStore.ts (navigator.onLine mirrored via the online/offline window events, drives ui/network/OfflineBanner.tsx); client state only, no Redux core/ App-wide settings (APP_NAME, VITE_API_BASE_URL), queryClient.ts (the shared TanStack Query client), and errorMonitoring.ts (a no-op unless VITE_SENTRY_DSN is set, which the default self-hosted Bugsink service sets automatically, see Error Monitoring) layout/ App shell: AppLayout, Navbar, Sidebar, ThemeToggle, LanguageToggle, FontSizeControl, navItems.ts. AppLayout takes an optional extraNavItems: NavItem[] prop so your own feature routes can add sidebar links without editing navItems.ts (upstream-owned), an optional extraNavbarContent: React.ReactNode prop so you can add your own top-bar content (buttons, icons, ...) without editing Navbar.tsx, and an optional onOpenCommandPalette: () => void prop that renders the navbar's search-trigger button for the command palette below. See Frontend Customization: shared-chrome extension points. Also CommandPalette.tsx (Cmd+K/Ctrl+K quick-jump: gated nav destinations, in-page content, and, if permitted, user accounts; result-building logic in CommandPaletteResults.ts, row rendering in CommandPaletteResultsList.tsx), mounted once at the app root in App.tsx alongside the global keydown listener that toggles it ui/ Generic reusable UI kit, no feature ownership. App-owned components use concrete folders that say what they contain: buttons/ (Button and button-variants.ts), inputs/ (Input, Textarea, PasswordInput and input-variants.ts), cards/ (Card), badges/ (Badge), links/ (AuthInlineLink), feedback/ (ConfirmDialog, FormAlert, LoadingState and result/tooltip helpers), navigation/ (Breadcrumbs, PageContainer, Pagination and section controls), filters/ (search, select, segmented and time-range controls), display/ (drawers, collapsible sections, glossary help and stat tiles), dates/ (dateFormatters.ts), and styles/ (classNames.ts, dialogStyles.ts, inputStyles.ts). Multi-file groups remain in their dedicated folders: DataTable/, table_actions/, toaster/, hooks/, network/, and routing/. hooks/ is the conventional React Hooks folder for useSomething files. The shadcn/ folder stays flat because each file is an independently generated Radix primitive. See List pages below translations/ translations.ts (react-i18next setup, NAMESPACES, SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES, lazy loadLanguage()), languages/<lang>/*.json namespace files, and the date and number helpers monthNames.ts, numerals.ts, timeOfDay.ts and searchText.ts. See Translations Overview theme/ tailwind.css is the Tailwind v4 entry point; it imports tailwind-tokens.css (theme custom properties and @theme mappings) and application.css (app-owned base, toast, scrollbar, and layout styles). applyBrandCssVars.ts/appearanceThemeOverrides.ts write the --brand-*/--bg-canvas-from/--bg-sidebar variables live when a signed-in user picks their own brand color or toggles light/dark; applyFaviconAndMetaColor.ts/brandIcon.ts update the favicon and theme-color meta tag to match. See Appearance for the full mechanism sdk.ts Public extension surface for your own feature code: the intended single import point for anything you build on top of this template, rather than reaching into the internal modules above directly. Groups roughly into: PBAC (PERMISSIONS, useAuthorization, useCan/useAuthorized, Authorized, IfCan, ProtectedRoute, authorizationService), API/session (api, extractApiErrorMessage, useAuthStore, queryClient, settings/APP_NAME, reportError), app shell (AppLayout, NavItem, Toaster, toaster), and generic UI components (LoadingState, Card, PageContainer, DataTable/DataTableColumn, ConfirmDialog, FormAlert, ErrorBoundary). See Using This Repository as a Template: the app/ + mystic_auth split This layout is feature/page-first, not a layer-first (components//hooks/services) MVC structure. A file's folder tells you which page or feature it belongs to, not what kind of file it is. Where a feature maps onto exactly one backend domain (auth/, authorization/), the folder names line up with the backend's own split (backend/mystic_auth/auth/, backend/mystic_auth/authorization/). That is a side effect of "one folder per thing," not the organizing principle itself. usePreviousLoginQuery.ts lives inside dashboard/ because Dashboard is its only consumer. UserStatsCard.tsx and PolicyStatsCard.tsx live inside users/ and policies/ rather than a separate stats/ domain folder for the same reason. api/, store/, core/, layout/, ui/, and theme/ are the exceptions. They are infrastructure or cross-cutting concerns with no single feature owner.

Zustand for client state: store/authStore.ts (isAuthenticated, name, email, role, permissions, hasPassword) and store/themeStore.ts (light/dark). No Redux. TanStack Query for all server state/caching, via one shared QueryClient (core/queryClient.ts). authStore.isAuthenticated starts as null ("not checked yet"), so App.tsx blocks rendering the router behind a loading screen until useAuthSession() resolves it to true/false, avoiding a flash of unauthenticated content.

api/axiosInstance.ts is a single Axios instance with withCredentials: true, using a base URL from VITE_API_BASE_URL. The JWT itself is never stored in JS-accessible state. See Authentication Overview. Per-domain typed call functions live in api/*.ts (auth_api, users_api, account_settings_api, policies_api, audit_api). api/apiError.ts shapes error responses uniformly. users_api.ts (policy-protected user management) and account_settings_api.ts (self-service PUT /users/me) are separate modules because they have different callers and permission requirements, mirroring the backend split into user_management_query_routes.py/user_management_update_routes.py/user_lifecycle_routes.py and user_self_service_routes.py. auth/session_lifecycle/setupAuthInterceptor.ts implements silent-refresh-on-401: a single in-flight refresh call is shared across concurrently-failing requests (no thundering herd of refresh calls), and login/signup/refresh/logout/reset/verify/oauth2 endpoints are excluded from the retry-after-refresh logic to avoid infinite loops. On an unrecoverable 401, it marks authStore unauthenticated and clears the cached GET /auth/me query. It does not handle 403; permission failures are left entirely to route/component-level guards (ProtectedRoute, Authorized, IfCan). It lives under auth/session_lifecycle/, not api/, since it's auth-session business logic that happens to configure the shared Axios instance, not a typed API call itself.

react-router v8 (see below for why not react-router-dom), BrowserRouter, defined in App.tsx. Only LoginPage is eager-loaded (the most common unauthenticated entry point); every other route is React.lazy-split.

Upstream stopped publishing react-router-dom past 7.18.1 and folded its exports into react-router for v8: everything except the RSC-only RouterProvider/HydratedRouter (under react-router/dom, unused here) now comes from the single react-router package. Not optional: react-router-dom@7.18.1 carried an unpatched high-severity advisory (GHSA-qwww-vcr4-c8h2) with no further release ever published under that package name. The fix only exists as react-router@8.3.0. Route Access Notes /, /dashboard authenticated DashboardPage /users USERS_LIST_ALL PBAC-protected user management /policies POLICIES_READ PBAC policy management /permissions PERMISSIONS_READ Permission catalog browser /rate-limits RATE_LIMITS_READ Rate limit dashboard /audit-log authenticated (self-service) "All users" tab gated separately inside the page /account-settings authenticated AccountSettingsPage.tsx; nav label "Account Settings" /login, /signup, /verify-account, /password-reset-request, /reset-password public /not-authorized public 403 landing, where ProtectedRoute sends an authenticated-but-unauthorized user * public 404 All protected routes are wrapped in ProtectedRoute, which redirects unauthenticated users to /login and unauthorized users to /not-authorized. AppLayout provides the sidebar and top-bar shell, so the shell renders only after access is confirmed.

Every lazy-split route in App.tsx uses ui/routing/trackedLazy.ts's trackedLazy() instead of plain React.lazy(). It wraps the same dynamic import() but calls startRouteLoad()/finishRouteLoad() (store/routeLoadingStore.ts) around it, incrementing/decrementing a pendingCount rather than tracking a single boolean, so two overlapping navigations (e.g. a user clicking a second link before the first chunk finishes) don't clear the loading state early. Two things react to that count: ui/routing/RouteProgressBar.tsx: a thin fixed-top indeterminate progress bar, mounted once at the app root, visible whenever pendingCount > 0. ui/routing/RouteSkeleton.tsx: the <Suspense> fallback for lazy routes. In practice this rarely renders, since React Router already wraps navigations in startTransition, which defers showing a fallback until the new route has had a chance to load; it exists for the rare case a route suspends before that deferral applies. ui/routing/RouteFadeIn.tsx fades each route's content in on every client-side navigation (mounted alongside the two above in App.tsx), so a route transition never pops in abruptly even on a fast, cached load. It deliberately skips that fade for the very first render after the static boot shell (frontend/index.html's pre-React "Loading your session" screen): fading real content in on top of the boot shell's own removal added a second, brief animated state between "boot shell" and "real page" that some visitors could see as two loading screens rather than one clean cut. The first paint after the boot shell is always instant, at full opacity; only a route change within the already-mounted app fades.

authorization/permissions.ts mirrors the backend's Permission enum as string constants, so route/component gates reference PERMISSIONS.USERS_LIST_ALL rather than a hand-typed string. authorization/useAuthorization.ts reads authStore.permissions and exposes can(action), failing closed (false) when unauthenticated or still loading. This is a client-side UX convenience only: the backend independently enforces every action via require_authorization (see PBAC Architecture); a hidden button is not a security boundary. authorization/ProtectedRoute.tsx, Authorized.tsx, IfCan.tsx: route-level and in-page conditional gates built on useAuthorization. authorization/authorizationService.ts layers real per-resource/conditional checks (POST /authorization/batch-check) on top of the cached flat permission list for cases that need it. role is explicitly treated as metadata only on the frontend too, never used in a gating decision, mirroring the backend's own design (see Security Decisions: role is never used to decide access).

Every policy-protected list page (UsersPage, AuditLogPage's four log views) follows the same pattern, server-side end to end: nothing is ever paged/sorted/filtered by loading everything and slicing it in the browser. To add another one: Pagination: track page in local state (useState(1)), fetch with limit/offset = (page - 1) * pageSize, render <Pagination page={page} totalPages={...} onPageChange={setPage} /> above and below the table. totalPages comes from Math.ceil(total / pageSize), where total is read off the backend's X-Total-Count response header (see API Reference: list endpoint conventions), not the page's own row count. Sorting: mark sortable DataTableColumns with sortable: true (the column's key doubles as the sort_by value sent to the backend, so it must match one of that endpoint's own allowlisted sortable columns); wire useSortState() into the table's sort/onSortChange props. Clicking an unsorted column sorts ascending; clicking the same column again flips to descending; clicking a different column starts that one fresh at ascending (standard spreadsheet convention). Filtering: a StyledSelect per fixed-vocabulary field (role, event type, allowed/success, ...) plus a debounced Input (useDebouncedValue) for free-text fields (email search, IP substring). An empty/"All ..." option maps to undefined, not an empty string, so it's omitted from the request entirely rather than sent as a real (and wrong) filter value. Resetting to page 1: any search/filter/sort change can make the current page invalid. ui/hooks/usePageResetOn.ts takes a single resetKey string concatenating every filter/sort value and compares it against its previous render. It uses the same "adjust state during render" pattern that PolicyFormDialog and UserAccessDialog use for reset-on-open, avoiding an extra render. UsersPage.tsx and every audit_log/ section component share it instead of reimplementing the same behavior. Backend counterpart: each such endpoint validates sort_by against an explicit allowlist (never a caller-supplied column name reaching the query directly) and computes X-Total-Count from the exact same filters as the row query, so the reported page count always matches what's actually being paged through. See user_base_crud.py and the two audit log repositories for the reference implementation.

Two different, deliberately different, rules govern when this app reserves space for a scrollbar versus lets the browser add one only when content actually overflows. Both are deliberate UI tradeoffs, not oversights - know which one applies before changing either. Page level: always reserved. theme/application.css's body rule sets overflow-y: scroll; scrollbar-gutter: stable;, and AppLayout.tsx's <main> repeats [scrollbar-gutter:stable]. This means the vertical scrollbar's ~14-17px gutter is present on every page, whether that page's content is tall enough to scroll or not. The reason: without it, navigating from a short page (e.g. Dashboard) to a tall one (e.g. Users with many rows) makes the scrollbar pop in and the entire page's content shift sideways by its width the instant it appears. Reserving the gutter permanently trades a constant, barely-noticeable strip for eliminating that shift - the same choice common production SaaS UIs make on their outer scroll containers. Do not remove this to "fix" the always-present gutter; it is solving a worse problem than it costs. Component level: reserved only when it can actually scroll. ui/DataTable/DataTable.tsx's scroll container and ui/filters/StyledSelect.tsx's .dropdown-scroll-area (see that class's own comment in theme/application.css) both deliberately leave scrollbar-gutter at the browser default (auto) instead of stable. Adding [scrollbar-gutter:stable] leaves a visible empty notch in the table's rounded corner whenever it had too few rows to need a scrollbar - since a table's or dropdown's own row count varies constantly (a filter, a search, or a user-management action) and there's no shared "user is navigating between different content" moment to protect against, unlike the page-level case, there's no reflow this gutter would be preventing, only wasted space it would be creating. If you add a new scrollable container inside a page (not the page's own outer scroll), default to auto and only reach for stable if you can point to the specific layout-shift it prevents.

Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui (Radix primitives). theme/tailwind.css is the stylesheet entry point; theme/tailwind-tokens.css defines the design tokens as plain CSS custom properties (a :root block for light values, a .dark-scoped block overriding what changes in dark mode, and an @theme inline block mapping them onto Tailwind utility classes). store/themeStore.ts + layout/controls/ThemeToggle.tsx handle light/dark switching by toggling that .dark class on <html>, independent of the OS-level prefers-color-scheme. theme/applyBrandCssVars.ts overrides the --brand-* steps (plus the two light/dark-dependent pairs, --bg-canvas-from/--bg-sidebar) at startup and on every brand-color change - see Appearance for how a pick flows through generateBrandScale.ts into those variables. Text size is a separate, independent control: store/fontSizeStore.ts + layout/controls/FontSizeControl.tsx (a navbar dropdown, small/medium/large) scale document.documentElement.style.fontSize as a percentage (87.5% / 100% / 112.5%), so it multiplies with whatever base size the user's own browser/OS already has set for accessibility, rather than overriding it outright. The choice persists to localStorage and is applied at module load, before the app renders, to avoid a flash of default-size text.

vite.config.ts uses Rollup's default automatic chunking, not build.rollupOptions.output.manualChunks. A prior version manually split every node_modules import into one vendor chunk (for better long-term browser-cache reuse: a deploy that only touches app code wouldn't have busted the cache for third-party code that hadn't changed). That was reverted after it broke the production-shaped local/self-hosted build: app code like api/axiosInstance.ts both imports from and gets imported by the vendor chunk, and Rollup placed shared CJS-interop helpers into axiosInstance's own chunk, creating a real circular chunk dependency. ESM's live-binding semantics for circular imports meant vendor.js called a binding from axiosInstance.js's chunk before that chunk's module body had run far enough to define it, throwing "TypeError: t is not a function" at the very top of the vendor bundle: the whole app failed to mount, a blank page with no build-time warning. See the comment in vite.config.ts for the full account. Re-introducing manual chunking is possible later, but only with verification in the local-prod/self-hosted mode (not just a local build) that nothing crashes. The main entry chunk doesn't trip Vite's "chunk larger than 500 kB" warning: each shadcn component under ui/shadcn/ only pulls in the specific Radix primitive it wraps, rather than one shared object bundling style recipes and machine code for every possible component regardless of whether the app renders it, so the bundle reflects what the app actually renders. Route-level code splitting is separate and already in place. See Routing above: every route except LoginPage is React.lazy-loaded, so route chunks only ever contain that page's own code plus the components it specifically imports.

VITE_API_BASE_URL (the backend's base URL), VITE_APP_NAME (the product name shown in the UI: navbar, auth pages, document title via index.html's %VITE_APP_NAME% substitution), VITE_BRAND_COLOR (the default brand color, see Appearance: Default brand color), and VITE_SUPPORT_EMAIL (contact address, undefined by default). All are Vite build-time env vars, read through core/settings.ts, and set in env/mystic_auth/.env.dev; running the stack via Docker, that's what the frontend container actually reads. frontend/.env.example only matters for running the frontend locally with npm run dev, outside Docker. SUPPORT_EMAIL is shared with the backend (also used as the Reply-To on outgoing email, see Background Email Delivery) and, on the frontend, appears on the Terms of Service / Privacy Policy pages and, once set, as a "Help & Support" mailto link pinned to the bottom of the sidebar (layout/app_layout/Sidebar.tsx) - the one spot every authenticated screen shares regardless of permissions, so it stays out of a fresh fork until SUPPORT_EMAIL is actually configured.

A 401 mid-session (expired access token) triggers one silent refresh-and-retry; a second failure marks the session invalid and, per route, redirects to /login. A session revoked elsewhere (logout-all, a targeted Manage Sessions revoke, password change) is pushed to every open tab within milliseconds via useSessionEventsStream.ts's SSE connection, not discovered only on the next request or poll. See Session Management: Real-time push. A 403 (authorization denial) is a normal API response the calling component/page is responsible for handling: typically a toast or an inline FormAlert, not a global redirect (except at the route level via ProtectedRoute). An uncaught render-time error anywhere in the tree (a bad API response shape reaching a component that doesn't expect it, a null-pointer bug, etc.) is caught by ui/routing/ErrorBoundary.tsx, mounted once at the app root in main.tsx (outside the router, so it also catches an error thrown before routing itself renders). Shows a "Something went wrong" fallback with a full-page reload action instead of React unmounting the entire tree to a blank white screen. Always logs to the console; also reports to core/errorMonitoring.ts (a no-op unless VITE_SENTRY_DSN is set, see Error Monitoring).
Tests live in tests/frontend/ (outside src/), not co-located. Vitest + React Testing Library + jsdom + axios-mock-adapter. See Testing Overview for the full breakdown and known coverage gaps.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Frontend Glossary. High-level overview of the whole stack. For the PBAC authorization pipeline specifically, see ../authorization/architecture/README.md; for deployment/runtime topology, see ../deployment/README.md.

Frontend: React + TypeScript + Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui (Radix primitives) + Zustand (client state) + TanStack Query (server state). Built as a static SPA, served by nginx in production-style Compose files or Vite's dev server locally (docker-compose.dev.yml). Backend: FastAPI, async throughout (SQLAlchemy async engine, async Valkey client). One process type (backend/app/main.py), shared by the backend, procrastinate_worker, and alembic containers via the same Docker image (docker/mystic_auth/dockerfiles/backend.Dockerfile) with different command: overrides. PostgreSQL: system of record: users, policies, policy history, both audit log tables (authorization decisions and security events), the Procrastinate job queue (procrastinate_jobs), durable token-version counters, and consumed refresh-token claims. Valkey: ephemeral/derived state only, never the source of truth for anything that must survive a flush: rate-limit/lockout counters and cached account/chain token-version counters (logout-all and single-session revocation), single-use password-reset/email-verification/OAuth2-state tokens (all with TTLs matching their expiry). Durable token versions and refresh-token replay claims live in PostgreSQL. Background jobs: Procrastinate uses the same Postgres instance as everything else (no Valkey broker). Auth flows enqueue email jobs with send_email_task.defer_async(...), and account lifecycle transitions enqueue downstream listener events. The procrastinate_worker handles delivery with retries and runs scheduled account purge, expired-session, refresh-claim, and passkey-challenge cleanup, and lifecycle-outbox reconciliation through its internal periodic-task deferrer; no separate scheduler process exists. Bugsink: self-hosted error monitoring, enabled by default: starts with the stack alongside everything else. Backend and frontend both report unhandled exceptions to it over the Sentry SDK wire protocol. Runs as its own container, using a second database on the same Postgres server (not a second Postgres instance). See Error Monitoring.

Valkey vs. Postgres: everything in Valkey is either a cache, a rate/lockout counter, or a single-use token: losing it on a restart degrades gracefully (a user re-requests a password reset; a rate limit resets) rather than corrupting state. Nothing that needs to survive indefinitely (users, policies, audit history, or the background job queue) lives there. Queued email: email delivery is the one slow, failure-prone I/O call in the auth flows. Queuing it means signup and password-reset requests are not held open waiting on SMTP. Procrastinate fits this stack because Postgres (already the system of record here) is also its job queue: no separate broker infrastructure. See Security Decisions: Postgres job queue. One backend image, three roles: backend, procrastinate_worker, and alembic all run from docker/mystic_auth/dockerfiles/backend.Dockerfile with different commands, rather than three separate images: keeps dependency versions/code identical across all three by construction, at the cost of the worker/alembic containers also containing an unused uvicorn entrypoint they never run.

Browser sends a request with access_token/refresh_token httpOnly cookies (never accessible to frontend JS: see Authentication Flows). SecurityHeadersMiddleware and CorrelationIdMiddleware/LoggingMiddleware wrap every request (see backend/app/main.py, backend/mystic_auth/auth/security/, backend/mystic_auth/logging/). Depends(get_current_user) (or, for a specific action, Depends(require_authorization(action, resource_type))) verifies the JWT, re-queries the user row (so a since-deactivated/deleted account is rejected even with a still-valid, unexpired token: see Security Decisions), and resolves the caller's current PBAC permissions from their assigned policies. On a 401 specifically, frontend/src/mystic_auth/auth/session_lifecycle/setupAuthInterceptor.ts attempts one silent refresh-and-retry before giving up and marking the session invalid: see Authentication Flows. The route handler runs, using authorization_service.authorize()/.require() for any access decision beyond "is there a valid session": every such call also writes an audit log row (allow or deny).
See ../database/design.md for the schema itself (tables, columns, foreign keys, and why several audit tables deliberately store user_email as a snapshot string rather than a foreign key).

This doc covers the full account-deletion lifecycle across backend, frontend, and the scheduled cleanup job: self-service delete (both the password-account and OAuth-only-account paths), permission-protected delete/reactivate/purge, and the automatic grace-period purge. It is split out of Database Design: Account lifecycle and Security Decisions: Product so the full flow, end to end, lives in one place with the sequence of each path made explicit.

Layer Files Responsibility Self-service route backend/mystic_auth/api/user_routes/user_self_service_routes.py DELETE /users/me, POST /users/me/confirm-delete Self-service services backend/mystic_auth/user_lifecycle/user_self_deletion_service.py, account_deletion_service.py, account_deletion_confirm_handler.py Shared soft-delete routine, deletion-confirmation token issue/verify, confirm-endpoint handler Permission-protected routes backend/mystic_auth/api/user_routes/user_lifecycle_routes.py DELETE /users/{email}, DELETE /users/{email}/purge, PATCH /users/{email}/reactivate Purge routine backend/mystic_auth/user_lifecycle/user_purge_service.py purge_user_account(), shared by the manual purge route and the scheduled job Lifecycle outbox backend/mystic_auth/user_lifecycle/account_lifecycle_events.py, account_lifecycle_outbox_model.py, backend/alembic/versions/f1a2b3c4d5e6_add_account_lifecycle_outbox.py Durable downstream event snapshot and at-least-once worker delivery Soft-delete mechanics backend/mystic_auth/user/user_crud_modules/user_lifecycle_crud.py soft_delete, reactivate, get_deleted_before(cutoff) Scheduled job backend/mystic_auth/procrastinate_tasks/account_purge_tasks.py Daily 03:00 UTC purge of accounts past their grace period | Frontend | frontend/src/mystic_auth/account_deletion/DeleteAccountCard.tsx, account_deletion/ConfirmDeleteAccountPage.tsx | Delete UI, password re-confirm, "check your email" state, the public /confirm-delete landing page | | Tests | tests/backend/mystic_auth/integration/user/, tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/user_lifecycle/, matching frontend suites under tests/frontend/mystic_auth/ | End-to-end and unit coverage for every path below | Each soft-delete, reactivation, and purge also queues a generic downstream account-lifecycle event. Purge writes the account_purged event; the account's prior audit history is left exactly as written, never anonymized (see Security Decisions: Infrastructure for why). See Background Email Delivery: downstream lifecycle extensions for the event contract and retry behavior.

Self-Service Paths: why there are two paths, and how each one works. Permission-Protected Actions and Purge: delete, reactivate, and purge actions gated by PBAC, plus the scheduled grace-period purge. Frontend: DeleteAccountCard and the /confirm-delete page.

Setting Meaning Default ACCOUNT_PURGE_GRACE_DAYS Days a soft-deleted account stays recoverable before the scheduled job purges it 30 ACCOUNT_DELETE_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES Lifetime of the OAuth-only-account confirmation link 60 Both are declared in the upstream-owned backend/mystic_auth/core/settings.py and set in the active env/mystic_auth/.env.dev<mode-suffix> runtime file (with any downstream-only values kept in the matching env/app/ file).

Backend integration tests cover both self-service paths (password re-confirm success/failure, OAuth-only send-and-confirm, expired/reused token, rate limiting on the confirm endpoint), permission-protected soft-delete/reactivate/purge, self-targeting and system-account guards, and that the scheduled job only purges accounts past their grace period. Backend unit tests cover account_deletion_service token issue/verify and user_purge_service.purge_user_account in isolation. Frontend integration tests cover DeleteAccountCard for both account types (password re-confirm validation, the "check your email" state) and ConfirmDeleteAccountPage's success/error/expired states.

Database Design: Account lifecycle: schema-level view of soft delete vs. purge, foreign keys, and cascade behavior. Security Decisions: Product: the why behind re-authentication requirements on both paths. Session Management: how session revocation (step 2 of every path above) actually works.

DeleteAccountCard.tsx (frontend/src/mystic_auth/account_deletion/) reads hasPassword off the current user to decide which flow to render: a PasswordInput re-confirm field for password accounts, or a plain confirm button for OAuth-only accounts. Either way it opens a ConfirmDialog before submitting. On success: If the response is { confirmation_required: true } (OAuth-only path), it shows a "check your email" state without navigating away, since the account and session are still both valid. Otherwise (password path), it clears every "me"-scoped TanStack Query cache (current user, sessions, own policies, own audit history, matching the same cache-clearing Session Management describes for logout) and navigates to /login. account_deletion/ConfirmDeleteAccountPage.tsx is the public /confirm-delete route the emailed link opens: it reads token from the query string, calls POST /users/me/confirm-delete, and shows success/error/expired states. It renders outside AppLayout/ProtectedRoute (like /login), since the caller may not have an active session on whatever device they open the email link from. See Account Deletion for the feature map.

All under backend/mystic_auth/api/user_routes/user_lifecycle_routes.py, mounted at /users: Route Permission Effect DELETE /users/{email} users:deactivate_any Soft-delete: same routine as self-service, permission-protected audit event (account_deleted). Same bump-failure handling as self-delete: the soft-delete always succeeds, an unconfirmed revoke is logged critical and recorded as sessions_revoked_confirmed: false in the audit metadata rather than erroring the request PATCH /users/{email}/reactivate users:reactivate Clears is_active/deleted_at; the only way to recover a soft-deleted account, whether self-deleted or deleted through a permission-protected route DELETE /users/{email}/purge users:delete_any Irreversible hard delete via the shared purge_user_account() users:delete_any is a distinct, more sensitive permission from users:deactivate_any, granted only by the seeded system_superuser policy: a caller who can delete accounts day to day cannot irreversibly destroy one. Both permission-protected routes reject the system account and the caller's own account as targets (a caller purging themselves through this route would be an unrecoverable lockout); self-service delete has no such guard, since acting on your own account is the entire point.

user_lifecycle/user_purge_service.py::purge_user_account(user, db, *, purged_by, request=None) is the one routine both purge paths call, so they can never drift apart: Revoke every session on the account. Unlike every other revoke-adjacent path in the app, this one fails closed: revocation happens before the irreversible hard delete below, so if the bump can't be confirmed (Postgres unavailable), purge_user_account raises TokenVersionUnavailableError and nothing past this step runs - no audit write, no delete. See Bump failure handling for why this one path is the exception to "the primary action still succeeds." Write the account_purged security audit event, before the row is deleted, since that event is what makes the irreversible action reviewable afterward. Hard-delete the row. user_policies rows cascade-delete (ON DELETE CASCADE); the account's historical security and authorization audit rows remain, with their original email/IP intact, never anonymized, as history with no foreign-key dependency on the deleted user (see Security Decisions: Infrastructure).

The scheduled job (account_purge_tasks.py::purge_expired_soft_deleted_accounts) is registered via @app.periodic(cron="0 3 * * *") and deferred automatically by the Procrastinate worker's own internal periodic-task deferrer: no separate scheduler process is involved (see Background Email Delivery). It queries user_lifecycle_crud.get_deleted_before(cutoff) for every account whose deleted_at predates now - settings.ACCOUNT_PURGE_GRACE_DAYS (default 30 days) and purges each one with purged_by="system:grace_period_purge". This is what gives self-service deletion (and permission-protected soft-delete) an actual recovery window, restorable via PATCH /users/{email}/reactivate for the whole grace period, instead of either purging synchronously (no recovery at all) or accumulating soft-deleted rows forever. See Account Deletion for the feature map, or Self-Service Paths for the user-initiated flows.

A hijacked access-token cookie (e.g. via XSS) should never be enough on its own to destroy an account. For a password account, re-submitting the current password is a cheap, immediate proof that beats the cookie alone. An OAuth-only account (hashed_password is None) has no password to re-submit, so it gets an async, email-confirmed equivalent instead, modeled on the existing password-reset flow: a signed, single-use link sent to the address on file. Both converge on the exact same soft-delete routine, so neither path can drift from the other in what it actually does to the account.
documents.s: Why there are two self-service paths

documents.t: user_self_service_routes.py::delete_my_account verifies current_password via the same password_service.verify_password call the change-password flow uses, then calls user_self_deletion_service.finalize_self_deletion(user, db, request), which: Soft-deletes the row (user_lifecycle_crud.soft_delete: is_active=False, deleted_at=now()). This Postgres write always succeeds, independent of Valkey. Revokes every session on the account (refresh_token_service.revoke_all_tokens_for_user, one account_ver bump, see Session Management). If the bump can't be confirmed (Postgres unavailable), that's logged at critical rather than raised: the soft-delete already happened, so there's no recoverable failure to report back to the caller, see Bump failure handling. Writes an account_deleted_self security audit event, distinct from permission-protected account_deleted, so the audit log can tell the two apart at a glance - its metadata carries sessions_revoked_confirmed so an unconfirmed revoke stays visible in the audit trail even though the deletion itself succeeded. The route then clears the access_token/refresh_token cookies on its response, the same shape logout_handler.py uses, before returning. All of this happens within the one request; the account is gone from the caller's perspective by the time the response arrives.

Send. DELETE /users/me on an account with no password mints a signed JWT carrying a type claim of "account_delete", scoping it away from access/refresh/reset tokens that share the same SECRET_KEY, so a valid deletion link can never be replayed as a login or password-reset token or vice versa. It's stored in Valkey under account_delete:{sha256(token)} with a TTL from ACCOUNT_DELETE_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES, then emailed as a link to /confirm-delete. The account and the calling session are both left untouched at this point. Confirm. POST /users/me/confirm-delete is deliberately unauthenticated (the token itself is the proof, the same trust model POST /auth/password-reset/confirm uses), so the link must work from whatever device the caller opens their email on, not just the one that requested deletion. Redeem. The token is redeemed via an atomic Valkey GETDEL, so two concurrent submissions of the same link can never both succeed; the first wins, the second sees the key already gone. Finalize. A valid, unexpired, unredeemed token runs the exact same finalize_self_deletion() routine as the password-account path (Path A above). Rate limiting. The confirm endpoint is separately rate-limited via login_protection_service under its own account_delete_confirm_lock:email: namespace, kept distinct from login_lock:account_ip: and password_reset_confirm_lock:email: so a stale or reused deletion link can never trip, or count towards, an unrelated lockout for that address. See Account Deletion for the feature map, or Permission-Protected Actions and Purge for the permission-protected and scheduled paths.
Split out of Authentication Flows to give the rate-limiting/lockout/timing-safety stack its own diagram; those three layers are the part of login worth seeing as a flow rather than a bullet list.

File Role backend/mystic_auth/auth/login/login_service.py, login_handler.py Credential check, ordering of rejection reasons, token issuance backend/mystic_auth/auth/security/rate_limiting/rate_limiter_service.py Per-IP and per-account sliding-window request limits backend/mystic_auth/auth/security/login_protection_service.py Brute-force lockout for an account/source-IP pair backend/mystic_auth/api/auth_routes/auth_routes.py POST /auth/login frontend/src/mystic_auth/auth/login/ LoginPage, useLoginMutation

Layered rate limiting. A generic per-IP sliding-window request limit (rate_limiter_service.py) runs before credential checks. A separate brute-force lockout (login_protection_service.py) counts failures for a normalized account/source-IP pair using MAX_FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP and LOGIN_LOCKOUT_TIME_PER_IP from env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example. The setting names are retained for env-file compatibility. Timing-attack-resistant comparison. login_service.py always runs the Argon2 comparison, against the real hashed_password if the account exists and has one, or a fixed DUMMY_HASH otherwise, before checking whether the account exists, is verified, or is active. "Wrong password," "no such account," and "account exists but is OAuth2-only (no password set)" all take the same amount of time to reject. Rejection order matters, separately from step 2. Once the (constant-time) hash comparison has run, login_service.py checks, in order: account not found, not verified, not active, and only then whether the password actually matched. This lets a legitimate user who mistyped their password on an unverified account see "verify your email" instead of a generic "wrong password," without weakening the timing protection above (the hash comparison already happened unconditionally). On success: issue a fresh access+refresh pair, set both cookies, log LOGIN_SUCCESS to the security audit log, and reset this account/source-IP pair's failed-attempt counter. On any rejected credential: log LOGIN_FAILURE and record a failed attempt. When a pair reaches its threshold, the next request is logged as login_ip_locked and receives 429. A lockout's 429 tells the caller how long to actually wait, not just that they're locked out: login_handler.py's _lockout_response reads the tripped lockout key's remaining Valkey TTL (login_protection_service.get_remaining_seconds) and surfaces it two ways, matching how production APIs generally communicate a 429's cooldown - the standard Retry-After header (RFC 9110) for any client/proxy that already understands it, and params.minutes in the JSON body (rounded up, never down to 0) for the login form to interpolate into its own translated message (errors.json's LOGIN_THROTTLED entry), since a raw header isn't user-facing copy.

tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/login/ covers the handler and service in isolation, including the rejection-order and timing-safety behavior; tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/security/test_login_protection_unit.py covers lockout independently; tests/backend/mystic_auth/integration/auth/test_login_integration.py exercises the full path against real Postgres/Valkey. See Testing Overview.

Authentication Flows: tokens/cookies and how login fits alongside the other flows. Session Management: what happens to chain_id/account_ver right after a successful login. Security Hardening: Abuse Prevention: the concrete rate-limit/lockout thresholds.

New to a term here? See the Authentication & Sessions Glossary. Split out of Authentication Flows. Both endpoints end sessions by bumping a durable Postgres version counter, not by deleting or blacklisting tokens; see Session Management: source of truth for why that scheme exists. This doc covers the two endpoints themselves and the idempotency behavior that makes them safe to call against an already-dead token.

File Role backend/mystic_auth/auth/logout/logout_handler.py POST /auth/logout: ends the current session only backend/mystic_auth/auth/logout_all/logout_all_handler.py POST /auth/logout/all: ends every session on the account backend/mystic_auth/auth/token_logic/jwt_service.py bump_chain_version / bump_account_version frontend/src/mystic_auth/auth/logout/useLogoutMutation.ts Calls /auth/logout, clears "me"-scoped query caches

Decode without verifying revocation. Both endpoints read the presented refresh token's claims via jwt_service.decode_payload, not verify_token, so they can still resolve the owning email and revoke whatever sessions remain even if the presented token is itself already stale (see idempotency below). Both still enforce the token's type claim, so a wrong-type token (e.g. an access token mistakenly presented here) is never treated as resolving a real session to revoke. POST /auth/logout bumps only that one session's chain_ver, ending just this device, and deletes the matching user_sessions mirror row (session_service.revoke_session_on_logout, functionally the same operation as a targeted Manage Sessions revoke, just triggered by the device ending its own session). This always returns 200 and clears cookies, even if the bump itself couldn't be confirmed (Postgres unavailable): the caller's own browser session is gone regardless, so that isn't treated as a failure, but the response body carries session_revoked: false instead of silently pretending the leaked token was actually revoked. See Bump failure handling. POST /auth/logout/all bumps account_ver instead. One Postgres increment ends every device immediately. The same mechanism backs refresh-token reuse detection for a pre-chain token and account soft-delete/purge. Unlike plain logout, revoking every other session is this endpoint's whole purpose, so an unconfirmed bump is not treated as a quiet success: cookies are still cleared (this browser's own session is done regardless), but the response is 503 SESSION_REVOCATION_UNAVAILABLE rather than 200, so the caller knows the other devices were not actually logged out. See Bump failure handling.

Neither endpoint treats "the presented refresh token is already revoked/expired/malformed" as an error: the caller's goal (no valid session left in this browser) is already true either way, so both still clear cookies (POST /auth/logout also still reports 200; see Bump failure handling for logout-all's own, separate 503 case above, which is about an unconfirmed Postgres bump, not a stale token). This matters concretely right after a self- or permission-protected password change, which bumps account_ver and revokes every session for the account, including the one the current browser is still holding. Clicking Logout immediately afterward presents that now-stale token; it must still log the browser out cleanly rather than surfacing an "invalid or already revoked" error while leaving stale cookies (and an apparently-still-logged-in UI) behind.

useLogoutMutation and the equivalent useLogoutAllMutation both call removeQueries (not just invalidate) for every "me"-scoped TanStack Query cache: current user, sessions, own policy assignments, own audit history. None of those caches are keyed by email, so leaving a stale response cached across a logout could otherwise flash the previous account's data for whoever logs in next in the same browser tab. See Session Management: frontend behavior.

tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/logout/test_logout_handler_unit.py and tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/logout_all/test_logout_all_handler_unit.py cover both handlers, including the already-dead-token idempotency case; tests/backend/mystic_auth/integration/auth/test_logout_integration.py and the session-management integration suite exercise both against real Postgres/Valkey. See Testing Overview.

Session Management: the version-counter mechanism both endpoints use, and how a revoked session is pushed to every open tab in real time. Authentication Flows: tokens/cookies and how logout fits alongside the other flows.
