New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary. How a scheduled backup flows from the database to off-host storage:

scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-backup/database-backup.sh and scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore.sh wrap Docker Compose, pg_dump, and psql. Every operator-facing database helper in that directory has matching .ps1 and .cmd entry points; those Windows wrappers delegate to the same tested Bash implementation through Git Bash. Use .sh from Bash/WSL/Linux/macOS, .ps1 from PowerShell, or .cmd from Command Prompt with the same arguments. Production-shaped Compose files use a custom pinned Postgres Alpine client image with a checksum-pinned rclone build, OpenSSL, and curl installed. Backups are encrypted with AES-256-CBC using PBKDF2 before they are written to ./backups; the key is never stored beside the backup files. The manual script accepts BACKUP_DIR=/path/to/writable/dir when the scheduled sidecar owns the default bind-mounted directory as UID 10001. The application database name is always taken from POSTGRES_DB in the selected mode's environment files. It is not required to be mystic_auth: downstream applications may use a name such as example_app_db. The encrypted backup round-trip test and restore-drill regression check follow the same setting and check the configured application database plus the separate bugsink database, so template and downstream runs exercise the same database-selection contract. Before keeping a dump, the backup script lists its contents with pg_restore --list. A dump of the application database with no tables is discarded and reported as a backup failure, since it means migrations have not run or the wrong database was dumped. The bugsink database stays empty until the Bugsink service has started once (CI and fresh dev stacks never start it), so an empty bugsink dump only prints a warning. CBC has no authenticated-encryption mode of its own (openssl enc -aes-256-gcm fails outright - the enc subcommand doesn't support AEAD ciphers at all), so scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/backup-hmac.sh adds the missing tamper-evidence separately: every <dump>.dump.enc gets a detached HMAC-SHA256 tag written alongside it as <dump>.dump.enc.hmac, using a MAC key derived from BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY (not the raw passphrase itself). backup-upload.sh ships the tag off-host with the dump automatically. database-restore.sh verifies the tag before decrypting a .dump.enc file - a present-but-mismatched tag aborts the restore; a missing tag (a dump made before this existed) only warns, so older backups stay restorable. Run scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/backup-freshness-check.sh from an external monitoring scheduler to verify that every required database has a recent, non-empty dump. It defaults to twice BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS and checks POSTGRES_DB plus bugsink; set BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS or pass the directory and maximum age explicitly when the deployment needs a different policy: BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS=30 scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/backup-freshness-check.sh /backups The check does not claim that an off-host object exists or that a dump can be restored. Use the restore drill for restoreability and monitor the B2 bucket itself for off-host freshness. Run scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/check-backup-encryption.sh periodically (or from the same external scheduler as the freshness check) to find plaintext .dump/.sql files and encrypted dumps with missing, empty, or malformed HMAC sidecars. This catches backup artifacts left behind during a format change even though restore itself tolerates a missing HMAC tag on an older dump (see above). The check defaults to ./backups; pass a directory explicitly to check another location. Set BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY in the scheduler's secret environment to also verify each HMAC against the ciphertext. Without the key, the script checks that each sidecar is well formed but cannot authenticate it. scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/check-backup-encryption.sh /backups When BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY is present in the scheduler's environment, the same command also verifies each tag against its ciphertext. # Dump the dev database and Bugsink database, if enabled scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-backup/database-backup.sh # Dump a production-shaped stack scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-backup/database-backup.sh docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml # Restore an encrypted dump, with confirmation scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore.sh backups/mystic_auth-20260717-120000.dump.enc # Restore without confirmation scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore.sh -y backups/mystic_auth-20260717-120000.dump.enc

Create a B2 bucket in the Backblaze dashboard with these choices: Give it a globally unique name, such as mystic-auth-backups-<owner>. Keep Files in Bucket set to Private. Enable Default Encryption. Enable Object Lock for a real backup bucket, then configure a 14-day Governance-mode default retention. Object Lock is irreversible, so leave it disabled only for a temporary test bucket. Backblaze's current signup offers 10 GB of free storage without requiring a billing method. Usage above the free allowance can still incur charges, so configure B2 caps and alerts. Create an application key with these choices: The key name is just a label, for example mystic-auth-backups. Restrict Allow access to Bucket(s) to this backup bucket. Select Read and Write. Leave Allow List All Bucket Names, File name prefix, and Duration empty. Copy the generated keyID and applicationKey. The key name is not a credential.

Dumps are the only recovery method; there is no point-in-time recovery. After a total loss you restore the latest dump and lose everything written since it was taken, so BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS is your data-loss window. The production example uses 1 (up to about an hour of loss). The freshness check alarms at twice the interval by default. Postgres managed services or WAL archiving (pgBackRest, WAL-G) are the upgrade path if an hour is too long. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) archives PostgreSQL's write-ahead log continuously so you can restore to a chosen second, such as just before an accidental delete. It is not enabled: it needs a tool such as pgBackRest or WAL-G (or a managed Postgres provider) plus log storage, key management, monitoring and restore drills, and archiving can fill the disk when its destination is down. Hourly dumps were chosen instead because the data changes slowly and the dump, HMAC, upload and restore-drill path is built and tested. Move to PITR when losing an hour of writes is unacceptable. The B2 bucket, application key and ownership are per-deployment. The freshness script cannot prove an off-host object exists, so the bucket needs its own monitoring and each deployment should repeat the remote restore check. Production-shaped Compose modes refuse to start without BACKUP_UPLOAD_COMMAND. The local-prod-ngrok B2 path has been tested by uploading both databases and fully restoring both from the downloaded objects. Two clean-up rules are independent of each other: Local files: BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS (14) deletes older dump files from ./backups. Hourly runs keep about 336 dumps per database for that window. B2 objects: nothing in this repository deletes them. Every dump has a unique name, so "keep only the last version" does nothing, and the bucket grows without limit. Add a bucket lifecycle rule in the Backblaze dashboard: hide files 30 days after upload and delete them 1 day after that. Keep the hide period at or above the Object Lock retention (14 days), or deletes will be refused. At hourly dumps that is about 720 objects per database in the bucket; multiply by your dump size to check it against the free 10 GB. Keep the application key in the deployment secret store, not in git. In the environment file used by the production-shaped Compose file, map keyID to RCLONE_CONFIG_B2_ACCOUNT and applicationKey to RCLONE_CONFIG_B2_KEY: B2_BUCKET=mystic-auth-production-backups RCLONE_CONFIG_B2_ACCOUNT=<keyID> RCLONE_CONFIG_B2_KEY=<applicationKey> BACKUP_UPLOAD_COMMAND=rclone copyto "$${DUMP_FILE}" "b2:mystic-auth-production-backups/$$(basename "$${DUMP_FILE}")" # Keep this in a secret manager and separately from ./backups. BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY=<64-character-secret> The doubled dollar signs are required in a Compose environment file so Compose passes the variable references through to the backup container. Use the real bucket name in both B2_BUCKET and the b2:<bucket-name>/... part of the command. Do not copy these credentials into an .example file. The scheduled db_backup image contains rclone; the manual backup command uses the same hook and therefore needs rclone installed on the host. Every dump is checked with pg_restore --list before this command runs. Dump, verification, and upload failures are reported through the same Sentry protocol DSN used by the backend. The scheduled service reads the generated Bugsink DSN from its shared Compose volume. For a manual host-side backup, export BACKUP_SENTRY_DSN if the host cannot read that volume. After configuring the bucket, verify both directions: make restore-drill scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-backup/database-backup.sh docker-compose.prod.yml rclone lsjson "b2:${B2_BUCKET}" rclone copyto "b2:${B2_BUCKET}/<dump-name>.dump.enc.hmac" /tmp/<dump-name>.dump.enc.hmac rclone copyto "b2:${B2_BUCKET}/<dump-name>.dump.enc" /tmp/<dump-name>.dump.enc scripts/mystic_auth/db/backup-verification/backup-hmac.sh verify /tmp/<dump-name>.dump.enc "$BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY" && echo "HMAC OK" openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -in /tmp/<dump-name>.dump.enc \ -pass env:BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY | pg_restore --list The restore drill in the repository checks a local dump. A deployment acceptance check must also download one named B2 object and restore that copy into a disposable database, then compare its schema and row counts. Periodic full dumps do not provide point-in-time recovery; use WAL archiving or managed Postgres if the backup interval is too large for the required RPO. The restore target is inferred from the dump filename. A bugsink-*.sql file restores into the bugsink database.
documents.s: Choosing the interval and cleaning up old objects

documents.t: docker-compose.prod.yml and every docker-compose.local-prod-*.yml variant run a db_backup service by default. Setting Purpose BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS Hours between scheduled dumps. BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS Local retention window for old dump files. BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY Required secret used to encrypt/decrypt .dump.enc files. Store it in a secret manager, not with the backups. BACKUP_UPLOAD_COMMAND Required in production-shaped modes; runs after each verified encrypted dump, with DUMP_FILE exported to it, to ship the dump off-host. ./backups Host directory where dumps are written. The sidecar waits for the alembic migration job to finish before its first dump. Every dump is also checked for at least one table: a dump with none (migrations not run yet, wrong database) is deleted, an alert is raised, and the next cycle tries again, so an empty file can never pass as a fresh backup. database-backup.sh applies the same check and fails the run. This is a periodic pg_dump loop with encryption, structural verification, and a fail-fast off-host upload requirement in production-shaped modes. scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-backup/database-backup.sh (manual/on-demand backups) honors the same encryption and upload settings for parity. The backup sidecar remains attached to the private postgres_net for Postgres access and also uses a separate non-internal backup_egress_net solely for off-host upload. It has no connection to Valkey's separate internal network. The scheduled backup image includes rclone and uses the B2 environment variables above. Compose sets RCLONE_CONFIG=/dev/null so the non-root backup process reads its credentials from the environment instead of trying the root-owned default config path. A host running the manual script needs rclone installed locally.

Operational boundaries: Production-shaped Compose modes fail to start without both BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY and BACKUP_UPLOAD_COMMAND; this prevents an unprotected deployment from appearing healthy. There is no point-in-time recovery - periodic full dumps only, so worst-case data loss is up to BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS of writes. Encryption protects backup confidentiality, but losing BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY makes recovery impossible. Escrow it separately and test recovery with the restore drill.

Each encrypted dump and its HMAC sidecar depend on the exact BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY used when they were created. Changing the configured key affects new backups and future restores; it does not re-encrypt existing objects. Keep each old key in a separate, access-controlled secret record until every backup made with it has expired or been deliberately removed. For a planned rotation, generate a new high-entropy key, update the backup service and the operator environment used for restores, then recreate the backup service so it reads the new value. Create fresh dumps for both POSTGRES_DB and bugsink, download one copy from the off-host store, verify its HMAC, and restore it into a disposable database before relying on the new key. Retain the prior key while any prior backups remain. If a key was exposed, treat backups made with it as potentially readable to anyone who obtained both the key and an encrypted dump; rotate the key and remove those objects when retention policy allows. Each dump is already verified with pg_restore --list immediately after writing, so a corrupt dump is caught before it's trusted, not after a restore is attempted. Beyond that structural check, run the restore drill periodically against production data to confirm the whole pipeline, not just the dump file, works end to end.

If there is no cloud account and no second server, use encrypted removable media as the minimum off-host path. # One-time repository setup on mounted removable media restic -r /mnt/usb-backup/mystic-auth init # After each backup restic -r /mnt/usb-backup/mystic-auth backup ./backups restic -r /mnt/usb-backup/mystic-auth forget --keep-daily 14 --keep-weekly 8 --prune Store the Restic password somewhere separate from the drive, such as a password manager. Disconnect the drive and keep it away from the host when possible. When a second machine is available, use the same repository model over SFTP: restic -r sftp:USER@REMOTE_HOST:/backups/mystic-auth init restic -r sftp:USER@REMOTE_HOST:/backups/mystic-auth backup ./backups Also keep a recoverable copy of the relevant env file, such as env/mystic_auth/.env.prod or env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok. A database dump without SECRET_KEY, database passwords, and provider secrets is not enough to recover the application.
documents.s: Off-host copy without a cloud account

documents.t: New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary. Startup order in the production-shaped Compose files:

The alembic service runs alembic upgrade head once and exits. In production-shaped Compose files, backend and procrastinate_worker wait for it with condition: service_completed_successfully, so request traffic does not start against an unmigrated schema. Before applying a migration in production: Review the migration file under backend/alembic/versions/. Pay special attention to dropped columns, altered types, data migrations, role changes, and destructive SQL. Confirm the migration has a downgrade only when rollback is actually safe. Run the test suite or at least the migration check in a production-like database copy. Migrations run with DATABASE_URL, normally the Postgres superuser. Runtime app traffic and Procrastinate task bodies prefer APP_DATABASE_URL, the least-privilege role created by migration. See Security Decisions: Least-privilege app DB role.

A migration backfill, or a one-off psql/support script, that changes who holds which policy or permission bypasses the normal API-driven cache invalidation: affected users can see a stale authorization decision for up to 60 seconds (_USER_POLICIES_TTL_SECONDS in authorization_cache_service.py). Run this right after any such write: # After an out-of-band UserPermission/UserPolicy change for specific users python -m mystic_auth.scripts.invalidate_authorization_cache --email a@example.com --email b@example.com # After editing a Policy's own definition (actions/resource_type/conditions), # which can affect every holder, not just one python -m mystic_auth.scripts.invalidate_authorization_cache --all-policies An API-driven grant/revoke never needs this - it invalidates the cache itself already.
documents.s: Invalidating the authorization cache after an out-of-band write

documents.t: The Compose files now use PostgreSQL 18. PostgreSQL data directories are not portable across major versions: do not start the PostgreSQL 18 image against a volume initialized by PostgreSQL 15, and do not remove the old volume as part of the upgrade. This is a dump-and-restore migration, separate from Alembic. Overview of the upgrade, with the old stack kept until acceptance: Before changing a deployment: Keep the existing PostgreSQL 15 stack running and take encrypted dumps of both POSTGRES_DB and bugsink with the existing release's backup script. Run the restore drill against that source stack and verify both dumps have matching HMAC sidecars. Copy the encrypted dumps and sidecars to storage that will remain available if the host fails. Choose a new, unique Compose project name for the PostgreSQL 18 stack. A different project name gives it a new postgres_data volume while leaving the PostgreSQL 15 volume untouched. Start only the new postgres service, restore the app and Bugsink dumps into it, and run the restore drill against the new project. Then start the complete new stack so its Alembic service applies any schema migrations. Verify backend readiness, frontend behavior, worker health, and the deployment-specific smoke checks before directing traffic to the new stack. Keep the old Compose project, release configuration, and data volume until the new stack has passed acceptance. For a production-mode candidate, substitute the selected mode's Compose file and env-file suffix in these commands. The project-name override is inherited by the helper scripts, so their docker compose exec calls target the new PostgreSQL 18 service: export COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=mystic-auth-pg18-candidate docker compose \ -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml \ -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml \ --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.prod \ --env-file env/app/.env.prod \ up -d postgres scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore.sh \ backups/<app-database-dump>.dump.enc docker-compose.prod.yml --yes scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore.sh \ backups/bugsink-<timestamp>.dump.enc docker-compose.prod.yml --yes scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore-drill.sh \ docker-compose.prod.yml docker compose \ -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml \ -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml \ --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.prod \ --env-file env/app/.env.prod \ up -d The examples use placeholders for the dump names. Keep the same BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY available to the restore helper that encrypted the source dumps. Schedule a maintenance window: both stacks cannot serve the same public ports at once, and the old application must stop writing before the final source backup. Do not run docker compose down -v on the old project. A rollback after the new database accepts writes needs a deliberate data-reconciliation plan; simply switching back would discard those writes.
New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary.

A backup nobody has tried to restore is a hope, not a guarantee. scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore-drill.sh proves both backed-up databases actually restore: it dumps the configured application database and bugsink, encrypts and authenticates each dump, then restores each into a disposable scratch database on the same Postgres server. It checks that the application schema and users table exist, compares public table names and row counts for populated databases, then drops the scratch databases. The development stack does not start Bugsink, so its separate database is empty there; the drill verifies that an empty Bugsink dump restores as empty. A populated deployment Bugsink database follows the same table and row-count checks as the application database. Concurrent drills do not collide, and cleanup never drops a pre-existing database. Neither real database is overwritten by the drill. It proves both backups restore without risking the data they protect. The drill reads both POSTGRES_DB and POSTGRES_USER from the selected environment (or the corresponding exported variables). Keep those values aligned with the database container; the scripts intentionally do not assume the role is named postgres. # Prove the dev stack's own database is restorable scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore-drill.sh # Same, against a production-shaped stack scripts/mystic_auth/db/database-restore/database-restore-drill.sh docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml Exits non-zero on any failure (dump, HMAC, restore, missing schema, or table parity), so a broken backup path fails loudly here instead of only being discovered mid-incident. tests/scripts/mystic_auth/db/test-restore-drill.sh runs this as a regression test in CI's browser-e2e Chromium desktop job, against both databases in the dev stack, on every push. It verifies the application restore, accepts an empty dev Bugsink database, and checks that both scratch databases are removed after the drill exits. This is how a real bug was found and fixed while building this drill: pg_dump --format=custom --file=- silently wrote a 0-byte dump on this image's pg_dump build instead of writing to stdout, and database-backup.sh used exactly that pattern. Both scripts now omit --file and rely on stdout redirection instead, which works portably regardless of that behavior. See the fixed line's own comment in either script for the detail.
This page explains how the backend's Python packages are pinned, why, and how to update them.

If only your direct dependencies are pinned, pip still picks the newest version of every dependency of those packages each time an image is built. Two builds a week apart can ship different code, and nothing checks that a downloaded file is the one you tested. A hijacked or re-uploaded package would install without any warning.

File Role Edit it? backend/requirements.in Direct runtime dependencies, pinned to exact versions Yes backend/requirements-dev.in Direct dev and test tools Yes backend/requirements.txt Generated lock: every package, including transitive ones, with --hash=sha256:... lines No backend/requirements-dev.txt Generated lock for the dev tools, resolved against the runtime lock No Installs always use pip install --require-hashes -r .... pip then refuses any package that is not in the lock, or whose file hash does not match. The Dockerfile, CI and local setup all install the lock, so they get the same packages. The lock is compiled with uv using --universal, so one file covers Linux glibc and Alpine (musl) and every Python platform the images use. uv is only a compile tool: it is not in the images.

Install the compiler once: pip install uv==0.13.7. Change the version in backend/requirements.in (or requirements-dev.in). Run scripts/mystic_auth/deps/compile-lock.sh. Run the full test suite, then commit the .in and the lock files together. To refresh every transitive package to the newest allowed version, run the script with --upgrade, then test the same way.

Lock is current: compile-lock.sh --check re-resolves and fails the build if a committed lock differs from its .in file, so the two cannot drift. Hashes enforced: CI installs with --require-hashes. Known vulnerabilities: pip-audit runs on the lock, so it audits the transitive packages too.

The frontend already has frontend/package-lock.json, which npm checks by hash. Update with npm outdated, then npm install, and run npx tsc -b, npx eslint ., npx vitest run and npx vite build. Check peer ranges before a major bump: for example typescript-eslint currently requires typescript <6.1.0, so TypeScript 7 has to wait for it.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary. Local development: hot reload on both backend and frontend, source bind-mounted from the host, no TLS. This is the mode you use day to day while writing code. Start here if you're new to the repo. Not sure this is the mode you want? See the dev vs. local-prod vs. prod comparison in the Deployment overview.

See Quickstart for the one-command version of all four steps above, with its own diagram. Want the whole thing in one command instead of the steps below? Run scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/quickstart/quickstart.sh (.ps1/.cmd): it does step 1 below automatically if env/mystic_auth/.env.dev doesn't exist yet, brings the stack up, offers to create the system superuser, then tails logs. See Template Usage: Quickstart. Step 1: Copy the env file. cp env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example env/mystic_auth/.env.dev cp env/app/.env.dev.example env/app/.env.dev Or run scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/setup-env/setup-env.sh (.ps1/.cmd) instead of a plain cp: it does this copy (and every other mode's) in one pass, generating a distinct random secret per password field and applying one app name/brand color choice everywhere. env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example is the template half for docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml; env/app/.env.dev.example is the downstream override half. It ships with the empty app-owned DEFAULT_APP_POLICIES extension point, and the MysticAuth defaults are enough to boot the stack as-is. It uses localhost URLs, development mode, Docker service names for internal database and Valkey access, and placeholder third-party credentials. To test session geolocation in dev, set GEOIPUPDATE_ACCOUNT_ID, GEOIPUPDATE_LICENSE_KEY, and GEOIP_DB_PATH=/usr/share/GeoIP/GeoLite2-City.mmdb. The dev-up.sh and PowerShell wrappers automatically enable the geoip Compose profile when that path is non-empty; the MaxMind updater then fills the shared volume before the backend is considered ready. Raw docker compose commands must include --profile geoip themselves. See Geolocation. Use a different template if you are not running dev: Local-prod: copy one of env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-{cloudflare,ngrok,tailscale}.example and use the matching docker-compose.local-prod-*.yml. See Local-Prod: which tunnel do I want?. Prod: copy env/mystic_auth/.env.prod.example and use docker-compose.prod.yml. See Choosing the right env template for the quick comparison. Step 2: Configure a login path. The stack can boot without real Google or SMTP values, but a normal user cannot finish signup and reach the dashboard until one verification path works: Configure FROM_EMAIL and GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD to support password signup, email verification, and password reset. Configure GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, and GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI to support Google login. Google login creates a verified account because Google has already verified the email. The CLI-created system superuser is separate from those normal-user paths. It is marked verified by the script and can sign in with its password without Google or SMTP. Regular password signups still need email delivery. See System Superuser for the interactive command, or local-scripts/mystic_auth/dev/create-system-user.* for a non-interactive version. See Environment variables below for the runtime rules, or the Template Usage Guide for the full first-run walkthrough (cloning, env/mystic_auth/.env.dev, and the first dev-up run). Step 3: Start the stack. ./scripts/mystic_auth/docker/dev/dev-up.sh # Git Bash, WSL, Linux, macOS .\scripts\mystic_auth\docker\dev\dev-up.ps1 # PowerShell scripts\mystic_auth\docker\dev\dev-up.cmd # Command Prompt The helper starts the stack detached, restarts backend and procrastinate_worker so their startup banners are fresh, waits for health checks, then tails logs from backend/frontend/procrastinate_worker. See Docker Overview: day-to-day dev-up helpers for why this is preferred over running the full dev Compose command directly. Run the full dev Compose command without -d when you want every service's logs interleaved into one stream, e.g. debugging Postgres/Bugsink/ Alembic startup itself rather than the app. Step 4: Open the app. Frontend: http://localhost:5173 API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs The Vite dev server sends CSP, frame denial, nosniff, referrer, and permissions headers. Its CSP allows Vite's development-time inline/eval scripts and the configured API origin; this is dev-only policy, not the production frontend policy. HSTS is omitted because this endpoint uses plain HTTP. Keep the published port loopback-only. If you expose dev over HTTPS or a tunnel, put it behind the production frontend proxy instead.

The paired env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example and env/app/.env.dev.example files are the source of truth for dev values. They include localhost URLs, Docker service names, development mode, and placeholders for Google, SMTP, and Bugsink. Dev values are read at container startup. If you change backend, database, Valkey, Google, SMTP, or rate-limit values in env/mystic_auth/.env.dev, restart the affected containers. If you change VITE_* values for the Docker frontend dev server, restart frontend so Vite reads the new values. See Environment and Runtime Configuration for what changes once you move to local-prod or prod.

All published to localhost for direct access: Service Port frontend (Vite dev server, HMR) 5173 backend 8000 postgres 5433 by default (POSTGRES_HOST_PORT) valkey 6380 by default (VALKEY_HOST_PORT) bugsink 8010

Source code is bind-mounted (./backend:/app, frontend/), not baked into the image. Edits take effect immediately. backend runs with --reload. No restart: policy beyond Postgres/Valkey. You restart manually. No alembic: service_completed_successfully gate on backend startup. No tunnel, no Caddy: everything is localhost-only, no public entrypoint. See Docker Overview: dev vs. production compose for the full service-by-service comparison across all three Compose files.

docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.dev --env-file env/app/.env.dev down Add -v to also drop the Postgres/Valkey volumes (wipes local data).

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary. Deployment modes use separate environment files so dev, local-prod tunnel variants, and prod can hold real values at the same time without overwriting one another.

Mode Copy this file To this file Use with Best for Dev env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example plus env/app/.env.dev.example env/mystic_auth/.env.dev plus env/app/.env.dev docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml plus docker/app/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml Local development with hot reload Local-prod Cloudflare env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example plus the matching app example matching env/mystic_auth/ and env/app/ files matching docker/mystic_auth/ and docker/app/ Compose files Your machine through Cloudflare Tunnel Local-prod ngrok env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok.example plus the matching app example matching env/mystic_auth/ and env/app/ files matching docker/mystic_auth/ and docker/app/ Compose files Your machine through ngrok Local-prod Tailscale env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-tailscale.example plus the matching app example matching env/mystic_auth/ and env/app/ files matching docker/mystic_auth/ and docker/app/ Compose files Your machine through Tailscale Funnel Prod env/mystic_auth/.env.prod.example plus env/app/.env.prod.example env/mystic_auth/.env.prod plus env/app/.env.prod docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml plus docker/app/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml Public server with Caddy TLS

# Dev cp env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example env/mystic_auth/.env.dev cp env/app/.env.dev.example env/app/.env.dev docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.dev.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.dev --env-file env/app/.env.dev up # Local-prod, ngrok example cp env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok.example env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok cp env/app/.env.local-prod-ngrok.example env/app/.env.local-prod-ngrok docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok --env-file env/app/.env.local-prod-ngrok up -d --build # Prod cp env/mystic_auth/.env.prod.example env/mystic_auth/.env.prod cp env/app/.env.prod.example env/app/.env.prod docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.prod --env-file env/app/.env.prod up -d --build The app-side examples are intentionally empty. Keep template-defined values in the mystic_auth runtime file and add product-specific values in the matching env/app/ file; do not edit tracked examples or tracked upstream Compose files.

The --env-file flag matters for local-prod and prod. Compose only auto-loads a file named .env in the working directory for ${VAR} substitution in Compose YAML, so the files under env/ must be passed explicitly. Each service's env_file: entry points at the correct dedicated file, but frontend build args and other Compose-level substitutions still need --env-file. Use the helper scripts when possible because they always pass the matching env file: scripts/mystic_auth/docker/dev/dev-up.* scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.* scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-ngrok/local-prod-ngrok-up.* scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-tailscale/local-prod-tailscale-up.* scripts/mystic_auth/docker/prod/prod-up.*

Setting group Read time Examples Backend runtime settings Container or process startup DATABASE_URL, APP_DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI, SMTP settings, rate-limit settings, DB_POOL_SIZE/DB_MAX_OVERFLOW, SENTRY_DSN Compose-only scaling setting Compose command evaluation, not read by the app itself UVICORN_WORKERS Frontend build settings Image build time VITE_API_BASE_URL, VITE_APP_NAME, VITE_BRAND_COLOR, VITE_SUPPORT_EMAIL, VITE_SENTRY_DSN, VITE_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT Compose interpolation settings Compose command evaluation Tunnel tokens, public domains, frontend build args, image names, exposed ports Production-shaped frontend values are baked into the static bundle by docker/mystic_auth/dockerfiles/frontend.Dockerfile. After changing any VITE_* input, rebuild the frontend image with --build.

scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/check-env/check-env.sh <file> (.ps1/.cmd) automates the part of this review a script can check: it fails if ENVIRONMENT=production but a secret still equals the shipped placeholder, or the required backup key/upload command is blank or the upload command does not reference $DUMP_FILE; it warns on remaining <your_...> placeholders or a host port already bound by something else. Run it before up, then review the rest of this list by hand: Review these settings before sharing a production-shaped deployment: Set ENVIRONMENT=production to disable /docs, /redoc, and /openapi.json. Generate real values for SECRET_KEY, GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, APP_DB_PASSWORD, and BUGSINK_SECRET_KEY. Configure at least one user verification path: SMTP email for password signup or Google OAuth2 login. Set FRONTEND_BASE_URL and BACKEND_BASE_URL to the public origin for the selected deployment. Set GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI to the exact registered callback URL. Set JWT_ISSUER and JWT_AUDIENCE, normally to the backend origin for this deployment. Set TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS to the reverse-proxy hop that should be trusted for X-Forwarded-For. For the bundled prod/local-prod-* Compose files this is derived automatically from FRONTEND_STATIC_IP/the tunnel's *_STATIC_IP var - see Routing: Trusted proxy IPs - so review those vars instead of TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS directly. Leave VITE_API_BASE_URL empty for the bundled same-origin nginx proxy, or set it only when the frontend is deployed separately. Set the app-owned DEFAULT_APP_POLICIES in the matching env/app/.env.<mode> file only when downstream app policies should be assigned to every verified user. Do not add it to env/mystic_auth. Configure SENTRY_DSN and VITE_SENTRY_DSN only when error monitoring is enabled. Configure GEOIP_DB_PATH and GEOIPUPDATE_* only when enabling the geoip Compose profile. Keep USER_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS sized for the largest safe CSV export your deployment can handle. UVICORN_WORKERS auto-sizes on boot and needs no default value; only set it to override the auto-picked count, and size DB_POOL_SIZE/DB_MAX_OVERFLOW to match if you do - see Scaling. For passkeys, set WEBAUTHN_RP_ID to the public hostname and WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS to the exact HTTPS frontend origin(s), or leave them blank to derive defaults from FRONTEND_BASE_URL. Keep the RP ID stable after users register credentials. See Passkeys.

Useful for iterating on the backend with a debugger attached, or a faster reload loop than the Dockerized dev target gives you. Postgres and Valkey still run in Docker either way; only the FastAPI process itself moves to the host. From the repo root, create a virtualenv and install both dependency files: pip install --require-hashes -r backend/requirements.txt -r backend/requirements-dev.txt. These files are generated locks; see Dependency locking before changing a dependency. Run scripts/mystic_auth/docker/dev/backend-host-run.sh (.ps1/.cmd). It starts only Postgres and Valkey, reads POSTGRES_HOST_PORT/VALKEY_HOST_PORT, derives the host-reachable URLs in memory, runs migrations, and starts Uvicorn with --reload. Pass extra Uvicorn arguments after the script path when needed. Settings (backend/mystic_auth/core/settings.py) reads env/mystic_auth/.env.dev and env/app/.env.dev directly when a variable isn't already in the process environment. The host-run helper supplies only the rewritten connection URLs and leaves the env files unchanged, so a single host-port edit works for both Docker and host-run workflows. Running the whole suite this way? tests/backend/conftest.py does the same postgres/valkey -> localhost derivation automatically from env/mystic_auth/.env.dev when DATABASE_URL/VALKEY_URL aren't already set, so pytest from the repo root needs no extra URL setup once the data services are running. See Testing Overview.

Self-hosted production image/runtime shape from your own machine or home server. The code is baked into images, reload is off, bind mounts are gone, and a free tunnel exposes the app to the internet without your own public IP, router port forwarding, or Caddy. Not sure this is the mode you want? See the dev vs. local-prod vs. prod comparison in the Deployment overview.

This base repository offers Quick Tunnels, Named Tunnels, ngrok, and Tailscale as alternatives for exposing the same local-prod app. Each has a walkthrough below; choose based on whether you need a temporary URL, a stable OAuth origin, a particular account/domain setup, or tailnet integration. The helper scripts already pass both the upstream and app Compose/env files. If you run a manual docker compose command copied from a walkthrough, add the matching docker/app/compose/docker-compose.<mode>.yml file after the docker/mystic_auth/ file and the matching env/app/.env.<mode> file after the env/mystic_auth/ file (.env.dev is the development exception). Cloudflare Quick Tunnel Cloudflare Named Tunnel ngrok Tailscale Funnel Account needed None Free, + your own domain Free; one assigned static domain Free URL stability Random; changes each run Stable Stable Stable Compose file None; points cloudflared at a local HTTP service docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml docker-compose.local-prod-tailscale.yml Env and token files None .env.local-prod-cloudflare and .cloudflare-tunnel-token .env.local-prod-ngrok .env.local-prod-tailscale Helper script cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:<port> scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.sh scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-ngrok/local-prod-ngrok-up.sh scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-tailscale/local-prod-tailscale-up.sh Walkthrough Quick Tunnel Named Tunnel ngrok Tunnel Tailscale Funnel Quick Tunnels are a fast, free option for a temporary demo and do not require a Cloudflare account or domain. Their random hostname changes on restart, so OAuth origins and callback URLs must be updated each time. Passkeys also use that hostname as their WebAuthn origin/RP ID: they work for the demo, but credentials registered under one Quick Tunnel hostname do not work under a new one. Update FRONTEND_BASE_URL and the WebAuthn settings after each restart if you want passkeys to work during the demo. They expose one local HTTP service, have no uptime guarantee, support at most 200 in-flight requests, and do not support Server-Sent Events. Anyone with the generated URL can reach the service. The Quick Tunnel walkthrough shows both a simple service demo and this app’s local-prod stack. Cloudflare Named Tunnel: uses a stable hostname under a domain whose DNS zone is in your Cloudflare account. It fits repeated demos and OAuth callback URLs that should not change. ngrok: the free plan includes one assigned static development domain, which can keep the demo origin and OAuth callback stable across restarts. The free tier has usage limits and an interstitial page. See its current plan details. Tailscale Funnel: publishes a service through Tailscale and can fit a setup that already uses a tailnet. Review Tailscale’s account and usage limits for your case. The three local-prod Compose tunnel variants produce the same app behind the same image/runtime shape: only the tunnel service, its Compose file, and its env template differ. Nothing about backend, frontend, postgres, valkey, procrastinate_worker, alembic, or bugsink changes between them. Not sure local-prod itself is the mode you want (vs. dev or prod)? See the dev vs. local-prod vs. prod comparison in the Deployment overview.

File Purpose docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml Production-shaped stack with an optional Cloudflare Named Tunnel service. The credential is a file-backed Compose secret. docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-ngrok.yml Production-shaped stack exposed by the ngrok service and NGROK_DOMAIN. docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-tailscale.yml Production-shaped stack exposed by the tailscale service and docker/tailscale-serve-config.json. env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example Cloudflare local-prod environment template. env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok.example ngrok local-prod environment template. env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-tailscale.example Tailscale local-prod environment template. scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.* Shell, PowerShell, and Command Prompt helpers that always pass both the MysticAuth and app-owned Cloudflare env files. scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-ngrok/local-prod-ngrok-up.* Shell, PowerShell, and Command Prompt helpers that always pass both the MysticAuth and app-owned ngrok env files. scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-tailscale/local-prod-tailscale-up.* Shell, PowerShell, and Command Prompt helpers that always pass both the MysticAuth and app-owned Tailscale env files. local-scripts/mystic_auth/local-prod-*/create-system-user.* Non-interactive system-superuser bootstrap helpers for each local-prod tunnel variant.

Each tunnel option has its own dedicated env template, matching its own Compose file, so all three (plus dev and prod) can have real values filled in at once without one overwriting another: Tunnel Copy this file To this file Cloudflare env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare Cloudflare tunnel credential env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token.example env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token ngrok env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok.example env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-ngrok Tailscale env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-tailscale.example env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-tailscale scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/setup-env/setup-env.sh (.ps1/.cmd) does all of these copies (plus dev and prod) in one pass, generating a distinct random secret per password field, instead of copying and rotating each by hand. Each is preconfigured for same-origin API routing and that Compose file's own fixed frontend nginx proxy IP. Rotate the secrets in the copied file before real use - scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/rotate-secrets/rotate-secrets.sh handles SECRET_KEY/BUGSINK_SECRET_KEY in place; the rest (POSTGRES_PASSWORD, APP_DB_PASSWORD, BUGSINK_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, VALKEY_PASSWORD) need a live-service step too, see its own header. Run scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/check-env/check-env.sh <file> before starting the stack to catch a leftover placeholder secret or an already-bound host port. Review FRONTEND_BASE_URL, BACKEND_BASE_URL, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI, SMTP, rate-limit, Valkey, and error-monitoring values before sharing the service. Production-shaped local-prod modes also fail closed until a direct security alert endpoint and both backup values are set: SECURITY_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL, BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and BACKUP_UPLOAD_COMMAND. The upstream examples include a generic B2/rclone upload command; fill in B2_BUCKET, the B2 credentials, and the encryption key in the gitignored runtime env file. The upload command must reference $DUMP_FILE and ship the verified encrypted dump and its detached HMAC to an off-host destination; the backup guide shows the same rclone form. Set the command in the gitignored runtime env file if your destination differs, then run the matching Compose config or helper before starting the tunnel. This is required even when the tunnel is only being used for a short local-production check. Build-time values must be final before you run --build: VITE_API_BASE_URL: keep empty for the bundled nginx same-origin proxy. VITE_APP_NAME: public app name shown in the browser (aliased from APP_NAME by the compose file - set APP_NAME, not this). VITE_BRAND_COLOR: default brand color (aliased from BRAND_COLOR - set BRAND_COLOR, not this). See Appearance: Default brand color. VITE_SUPPORT_EMAIL: contact address on the Terms of Service / Privacy Policy pages and, once set, a "Help & Support" link in the sidebar (aliased from SUPPORT_EMAIL - set SUPPORT_EMAIL, not this). VITE_SENTRY_DSN: public browser DSN if frontend error reporting is enabled. VITE_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: frontend environment tag. Runtime values can be changed with a container restart: SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL, POSTGRES_*, VALKEY_URL, and VALKEY_PASSWORD FRONTEND_BASE_URL, BACKEND_BASE_URL, GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI SMTP settings, rate-limit settings, and backend SENTRY_DSN WEBAUTHN_RP_ID, WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS, and WEBAUTHN_RP_NAME; keep the RP ID stable after passkeys are registered VITE_API_BASE_URL, VITE_APP_NAME, VITE_SUPPORT_EMAIL, VITE_SENTRY_DSN, and VITE_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT are baked in at image build time, not read at container runtime. Set them (or their aliased APP_NAME/SUPPORT_EMAIL source vars) in your chosen tunnel's env file before --build, not after. Always run Compose with --env-file pointed at that same file (or the matching scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-*/local-prod-*-up.sh / .ps1 / .cmd helper, which does this for you) - without it, ${VAR} build-arg substitution silently falls back to whatever's in env/mystic_auth/.env.dev instead. See Environment and Runtime Configuration for the full explanation of each. Session geolocation (GEOIP_DB_PATH/GEOIPUPDATE_*) is covered as an optional step in each tunnel's own walkthrough, since it needs an extra flag on the "start the stack" command in each.

See Docker Overview: dev vs. production compose for the full table. In short: no bind mounts, no reload, unless-stopped restart policy, alembic gates backend/procrastinate_worker startup, and TLS terminates at the tunnel provider's edge rather than in a container you run. Use docker-compose.prod.yml instead (see Prod Deployment) if you'd rather the host itself own the public IP and terminate TLS via Caddy, for example on your own server.

Each of the three Compose files sets its own: name: (COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME) network subnet (DOCKER_SUBNET: 172.28.0.0/24 Cloudflare, 172.30.0.0/24 ngrok, 172.31.0.0/24 Tailscale by default) host port range (*_HOST_PORT: backend/frontend 8001/8080 Cloudflare, 8101/8180 ngrok, 8201/8280 Tailscale by default) so all three - plus dev and prod - can run on the same Docker host at once with zero container, network, volume, or port collision. Useful for comparing tunnel options side by side, or just because a stray container from one variant is still up while you start another. These are all env vars with no built-in fallback, set in each env/mystic_auth/.env*.example - see Docker: Compose Modes for why.

documents.t: See Local-Prod Deployment for the mode chooser, environment variables, and how local-prod differs from dev/prod. This page is the stable-URL Cloudflare Named Tunnel walkthrough, start to finish.

File Why it matters docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml Defines the stack and runs Cloudflare Named Tunnel by default. env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example Source template for Cloudflare local-prod application settings. env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token.example Empty secret-file template. Copy it to .cloudflare-tunnel-token and place the tunnel token there. env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare Your local, gitignored copy with the public hostname, Google callback, and application secrets. scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.* Compose helpers that always pass the Cloudflare env file. local-scripts/mystic_auth/local-prod-cloudflare/create-system-user.* Optional non-interactive system-superuser creation scripts.

Requires a domain added to a free Cloudflare account. The domain's DNS zone must live in your own Cloudflare account for tunnel routing to work. A subdomain donated by a third-party registry repo (is-a.dev, rweb.site, etc.) will not work here, since Cloudflare Tunnel resolves the target tunnel by matching the request against Public Hostname config in the account that owns the zone: a zone you don't control can't route to a tunnel it doesn't know about. If you want a custom hostname and do not own a domain yet, you can buy one from a registrar and delegate its DNS to your Cloudflare account. For a short demo without a custom domain, use a Quick Tunnel. Cloudflare Named Tunnel authenticates with a persistent token mounted from a file-backed Compose secret. The repository builds a pinned Cloudflare source release with the patched klauspost/compress dependency and includes a readiness health check. The token never enters the container environment or process arguments. Traffic enters Cloudflare at https://your-hostname, then Cloudflare routes that hostname to the named tunnel, and cloudflared forwards it to http://frontend:80 inside Docker. Step 1: Copy the env files and create the token secret file. cp env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare cp env/app/.env.local-prod-cloudflare.example env/app/.env.local-prod-cloudflare cp env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token.example env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token chmod 600 env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token On Windows PowerShell, restrict the file ACL instead of using chmod: icacls env\mystic_auth\.cloudflare-tunnel-token /inheritance:r /grant:r "$([System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().Name):(R)" "SYSTEM:(R)" "BUILTIN\Administrators:(R)" Keep the token file out of git. The startup helper checks that it exists, is non-empty, and restricts access to your account, SYSTEM, and Administrators on Windows. On Unix it requires no group/world permissions. Paste the token from the Cloudflare Zero Trust install screen into this file, not the .env file. This Compose file includes a Named Tunnel service. For a temporary Quick Tunnel demo with the same app stack, follow the Quick Tunnel walkthrough, which starts the frontend and app services without starting cloudflared. Do not start local-prod from env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example; that file is for the dev stack. Step 2: Create the tunnel in Cloudflare. Zero Trust dashboard → Networks → Tunnels → Create a tunnel → Cloudflared → name it. Copy the token shown in the install step into env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token. Step 3: Point the tunnel at your app. Still in that tunnel's config: Public Hostname → Add a public hostname → your domain or subdomain → Service: HTTP → http://frontend:80. Step 4: Point the app at that hostname. In env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare, set FRONTEND_BASE_URL and BACKEND_BASE_URL to https://your-hostname once it's live. Leave VITE_API_BASE_URL empty: frontend and backend share one public origin behind the tunnel, and nginx (docker/mystic_auth/nginx.frontend.conf) proxies API prefixes to backend same-origin, so the browser never needs a separate API URL. Set WEBAUTHN_RP_ID=your-hostname and WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS=https://your-hostname for passkeys. Keep the hostname and RP ID stable after users enroll credentials; see Passkeys. Also set JWT_ISSUER and JWT_AUDIENCE to https://your-hostname. They don't have to match FRONTEND_BASE_URL for tokens to work (they're only checked against themselves, see Authentication Overview), but leaving them at the placeholder default means every deployment that copies this tutorial mints tokens with the same iss/aud. Step 5: Register the hostname with Google and enable Google login. In the Google Cloud Console, under APIs & Services, Credentials, your OAuth 2.0 Client ID, add https://your-hostname/auth/oauth2/callback/google under Authorized redirect URIs and https://your-hostname under Authorized JavaScript origins. Then set GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI in env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare to that same redirect URI. It must match byte-for-byte, or login fails with redirect_uri_mismatch. Step 6: Start the stack. ./scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.sh # PowerShell: .\scripts\mystic_auth\docker\local-prod-cloudflare\local-prod-cloudflare-up.ps1 Open https://your-hostname in a browser: that's your app, live at a stable address. Unlike Quick Tunnel, this URL doesn't change, so Steps 4 and 5 are one-time setup, not something you repeat on every restart. See OAuth2 / PKCE if login still fails after this. Step 7b (Optional): Enable session geolocation. Setting GEOIP_DB_PATH/GEOIPUPDATE_ACCOUNT_ID/GEOIPUPDATE_LICENSE_KEY in env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare alone does nothing: the geoipupdate service that downloads the .mmdb file is gated behind the geoip Compose profile, skipped by the startup command as written. Re-run the helper with the profile added instead: ./scripts/mystic_auth/docker/local-prod-cloudflare/local-prod-cloudflare-up.sh --profile geoip up -d --build Without it, the updater is not started and Manage Sessions' Location column shows "Unknown". When the profile is enabled, the updater healthcheck requires a non-empty database and becomes unhealthy if the download fails. See Session Geolocation for the MaxMind account/license-key setup this depends on.

Symptom Cause Fix Cloudflare hostname returns 404 or tunnel not found Public Hostname is not attached to the tunnel whose token is in .cloudflare-tunnel-token. In Cloudflare Zero Trust, open the tunnel, then verify Public Hostname points to http://frontend:80. DNS does not resolve your hostname Domain nameservers are not delegated to your Cloudflare account or DNS has not propagated yet. Check the domain in Cloudflare DNS and wait for delegation. New domains can take longer than the tunnel setup itself. cloudflared exits immediately The token file is missing, empty, or invalid. Put the token from the tunnel install step in env/mystic_auth/.cloudflare-tunnel-token, keep Unix permissions at 0600, then restart the stack. Google login returns redirect_uri_mismatch Google Cloud Console callback does not match GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI. Register https://your-hostname/auth/oauth2/callback/google under Authorized redirect URIs. API calls return 502 after changing backend env values nginx cached the previous backend container IP. Recreate backend and frontend together with --force-recreate.

Cloudflare Quick Tunnels are free and require no Cloudflare account or domain. They are useful for a short demo or for sharing one local HTTP service. A Quick Tunnel gets a random trycloudflare.com hostname each time it starts. That makes it a poor fit for OAuth providers that require a registered callback URL: you must update the provider's allowed origin and callback URL, and the app's public URL settings, every time the hostname changes. Passkeys can still be used for a short demo, but their relying-party identity is tied to that hostname. Credentials enrolled at one Quick Tunnel URL stop working when the next URL changes. Set FRONTEND_BASE_URL (or explicitly set WEBAUTHN_RP_ID and WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS) to the current public URL before enrolling passkeys. See Passkey domain configuration. This repository is a base with several tunnel choices. Pick the one that fits your demo: use Quick Tunnel for a fast, temporary URL; use a stable ngrok domain if its free domain meets your needs; use Tailscale Funnel if you already use Tailscale; or use a Cloudflare Named Tunnel with a domain in your Cloudflare account. See the comparison. Cloudflare documents Quick Tunnels as temporary and without an uptime guarantee. They support up to 200 in-flight requests, do not support Server-Sent Events, and expose the selected local service to anyone who has the URL. See Cloudflare's Quick Tunnel guide.

These steps work on Linux, WSL, and Windows PowerShell. Install cloudflared from Cloudflare's download page. No login or cloudflared tunnel login is needed for a Quick Tunnel. Start the service you want to share. For a simple smoke demo from the repository root, serve the documentation directory on port 8080: python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory docs In Windows PowerShell, use: py -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory docs Open a second terminal and start the tunnel to that local port: cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080 In Windows PowerShell, the executable may be named cloudflared.exe: cloudflared.exe tunnel --url http://localhost:8080 Wait for the https://<random-name>.trycloudflare.com URL in the output, then open it in a browser or share it with your demo audience. The tunnel forwards to the one local service and port from step 2. To stop sharing, press Ctrl+C in the cloudflared terminal and stop the local service. Starting another Quick Tunnel creates a different URL. For a small extra access check, Cloudflare supports an email PIN gate with --allowed-mail: cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080 --allowed-mail alice@example.com The recipient must enter the one-time PIN sent to that address. This is a convenience gate for a demo, not a replacement for the app's own authentication.
documents.s: Quick demo: share a local HTTP service

documents.t: The local-prod Cloudflare Compose file normally includes the Named Tunnel service. To use a Quick Tunnel instead, start the same app stack while naming the app services explicitly, which leaves the cloudflared service stopped; then run the Quick Tunnel on the host to the frontend port. The frontend's nginx serves the built app and proxies API paths to the backend on the same origin. Install Docker with Compose and cloudflared, then prepare local-prod env files using the repository setup helper. From the repository root run one of: ./scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/setup-env/setup-env.sh .\scripts\mystic_auth\env-tools\setup-env\setup-env.ps1 The helper prepares all mode-specific env files. Fill the local-prod Cloudflare and app env files with the required values described in Local-Prod Deployment, and run scripts/mystic_auth/env-tools/check-env/check-env.sh (or its PowerShell counterpart) on the two files. The Named Tunnel token is not used by the selected app services; this walkthrough does not start cloudflared. Build and start the local-prod services except cloudflared. Run from the repository root: docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare --env-file env/app/.env.local-prod-cloudflare up -d --build postgres valkey bugsink bugsink-seed alembic backend frontend procrastinate_worker db_backup This uses the repo's Cloudflare local-prod app configuration but does not start the Named Tunnel. The frontend is published on the port configured by FRONTEND_HOST_PORT (8080 in the example env file). In another terminal, publish that local frontend port through a Quick Tunnel. On the default port, use the command from the quick-demo section: cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080 Open the generated HTTPS URL. Keep both the Compose stack and cloudflared running while the demo is in use. Stop cloudflared with Ctrl+C when finished, then stop the app stack: docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare --env-file env/app/.env.local-prod-cloudflare down Set FRONTEND_BASE_URL, BACKEND_BASE_URL, JWT_ISSUER, and JWT_AUDIENCE to the generated HTTPS origin in env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare. Blank WEBAUTHN_RP_ID and WEBAUTHN_ORIGINS derive from FRONTEND_BASE_URL; keep them blank or set them to the exact current hostname and origin before enrolling passkeys. Rebuild the backend and frontend with the updated settings: docker compose -f docker/mystic_auth/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml -f docker/app/compose/docker-compose.local-prod-cloudflare.yml --env-file env/mystic_auth/.env.local-prod-cloudflare --env-file env/app/.env.local-prod-cloudflare up -d --build backend frontend If Google OAuth is enabled, also register the random public hostname with Google as an authorized JavaScript origin and redirect URI, and set GOOGLE_REDIRECT_URI to https://<random-name>.trycloudflare.com/auth/oauth2/callback/google. Repeat the public URL updates and rebuild when the Quick Tunnel hostname changes. Passkeys enrolled at the previous hostname cannot be used at the new one, so enroll a new passkey there before removing the old credential. For a demo without OAuth, skip the Google registration and use another account setup already configured in your environment.
