Expired claim rows are removed by a daily bounded cleanup task. Covered by the JTI unit tests and real PostgreSQL integration tests, including replay after deleting any legacy Valkey marker.

Every access and refresh token embeds the account's account_ver and its own chain's chain_ver at mint time (jwt_service.py). verify_token and refresh_tokens() compare those values with durable Postgres records; Valkey is only a best-effort cache. A whole-account revoke (POST /auth/logout/all, password reset confirm, self/protected password change, forced deactivation/purge) is one bump_account_version call. One atomic Postgres upsert increment makes every device's access and refresh tokens fail on their next use, with no per-token iteration. A single-session revoke (logout, a targeted Manage Sessions "End session", or chain-scoped reuse containment above) is the equivalent durable Postgres bump_chain_version, scoped to one chain. What this replaced: a design that tracked every live refresh-token jti in a per-user Valkey Hash (to revoke by iterating it) plus a separate "access tokens issued before this timestamp are dead" epoch key for access tokens specifically. That epoch mechanism had a real, self-inflicted bug: PyJWT truncates a datetime-valued iat claim to whole seconds while encoding, but the epoch itself kept full sub-second precision. So a token minted the moment after a revoke (e.g. logging back in immediately after logout-all, trivially easy since the two calls are naturally back-to-back) could still decode to an iat numerically less than the epoch, and come back rejected as if it predated a revocation it actually postdated. The fix at the time (encoding iat as a raw float instead of a datetime, preserving real ordering) is now moot: the version-based comparison this section describes is a plain integer equality check with no timestamp precision involved at all, so that whole class of bug can't recur. See tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/token_logic/test_jwt_service_unit.py.
documents.s: Revocation is version-based: one durable Postgres version bump, not a token registry to iterate

documents.t: State + PKCE: a random state (Valkey + cookie, validated on callback, single-use via atomic GETDEL) plus PKCE (S256), exceeding the minimum CSRF protection a plain OAuth2 state parameter alone would provide. email_verified is load-bearing: an OAuth2 login is only trusted if Google's own email_verified flag is true. This is the only proof of address ownership the flow relies on. Pre-registration hijack window: if an attacker signs up with a victim's email (password-based, unverified) before the victim ever does, and the victim later authenticates via Google with that same address, the pre-existing account's password is cleared at that moment. Without this, the attacker's chosen password would remain valid on an account Google has now confirmed belongs to someone else. See Google OAuth2 / PKCE for the full walkthrough. Redirect URI is server-side fixed, never client-influenced, ruling out open-redirect-via-OAuth.

user_crud.get_by_email (existence check) and user_crud.create are not wrapped in a single atomic transaction in either signup_service.py or oauth2_service.py, so a TOCTOU race between two concurrent requests for the same new email is theoretically possible at the application level. The database closes it with a unique constraint on users.email, so the loser gets an IntegrityError. Both call sites catch broad exceptions, log, and return a clean failure (False or None) that the handler turns into the standard generic error response.

PUT /users/me (self-service profile update) requires current_password, verified against the account's existing hashed_password, whenever the request also sets a new password. Without this, a hijacked access_token cookie (e.g. via XSS) was enough to permanently lock the legitimate owner out: the attacker just sets a new password, no proof of the old one required, and the existing "password change revokes all sessions" behavior (see ../database/design.md) would then work against the real owner by killing their session too. Skipped when the account has no password yet (hashed_password is None, an OAuth-only account setting a password for the first time): there's nothing to confirm against, and requiring one would make it impossible for such an account to ever add a password. The protected account route (PUT /users/{email}, which reuses the same UserUpdate schema) does not require this, since a caller changing someone else's password already authenticated via their own users:update_any permission; requiring the target's current password there would be nonsensical and isn't what the check is protecting against. See backend/mystic_auth/api/user_routes/user_self_service_routes.py::update_my_profile and tests/backend/mystic_auth/integration/user/test_user_self_service_routes_integration.py (test_self_password_change_requires_current_password, test_self_password_change_rejects_wrong_current_password, test_setting_a_first_password_on_an_oauth_only_account_does_not_require_current_password) and test_user_account_lifecycle_integration.py (test_management_password_change_does_not_require_admins_current_password).
documents.s: Self-service password change requires the current password

documents.t: The rejected design: treating "the presented refresh token is already revoked/expired/malformed" as a 400 error without clearing cookies. Why that matters: it is reachable through a completely legitimate path, not just an attacker replaying a stale token. A self-service or permission-protected password change (see below) revokes every refresh token for the account, including the one the current browser is still holding. So clicking Logout right after a "password updated" toast presented that now-dead token, got a 400 Invalid refresh token or already revoked, and was left looking still logged in with stale cookies the client had no way to clear itself (setupAuthInterceptor.ts only acts on 401, and useLogoutMutation's onSuccess, the only place that clears the Zustand auth store, never fires on a mutation error). The chosen behavior: both handlers treat this as a success. The caller's actual goal, no valid session left in this browser, is already true whether or not the presented token was still live to revoke, so both always clear cookies and return 200. logout/all uses jwt_service.decode_payload instead of jwt_service.verify_token (which refuses to return anything for an already-revoked token) (which skips the revocation check, same as reuse-detection in refresh_token_service.py), so it can still resolve the owning email and revoke whatever sessions remain elsewhere, while still enforcing the token's type claim, so a wrong-type token (e.g. an access token mistakenly presented as the refresh cookie) is never treated as resolving a real session. The security audit trail is unaffected by the response-code change: both handlers still record success=False for an already-dead/undecodable token (and, for logout/all, user_email=None when no email could be recovered at all), so a real operator reviewing the log can still tell the two cases apart even though the caller-facing outcome looks identical. Scope of the idempotency: this is specifically about an already-dead presented token, not about whether the revoke Valkey was asked to perform actually happened. logout/all is the one exception to "always 200": if the account-version bump itself can't be confirmed (Postgres unavailable), it returns 503 instead, since unlike an already-dead token (nothing left to revoke, goal already met) an unconfirmed bump means the revoke genuinely didn't happen. Plain logout keeps returning 200 even then, since ending this one browser's own session is its actual goal regardless of the wider account state. See Session Management: bump failure handling. Also covered: The permission-protected path, not just self-service: a caller changing a different account's password (PUT /users/{email}) revokes that target's sessions, so the target's own browser is the one left holding a dead refresh-token cookie; logging out from the target's session must succeed the same way. A malformed (not just merely-revoked) cookie value. Two logout calls presenting the identical already-used token back to back (e.g. two tabs, or a retried request): both must succeed rather than only the first. See backend/mystic_auth/auth/logout/logout_handler.py, backend/mystic_auth/auth/logout_all/logout_all_handler.py, tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/logout/test_logout_handler_unit.py, tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/logout_all/test_logout_all_handler_unit.py, and tests/backend/mystic_auth/integration/user/test_user_self_service_routes_integration.py (test_logout_after_self_password_change_still_succeeds_and_clears_cookies, test_logout_all_after_self_password_change_still_succeeds_and_clears_cookies, test_repeated_logout_calls_with_the_same_token_both_succeed, test_logout_with_malformed_refresh_token_cookie_still_succeeds_and_clears_cookies, test_logout_all_with_malformed_refresh_token_cookie_still_succeeds_and_clears_cookies) and test_user_account_lifecycle_integration.py (test_logout_after_admin_password_change_for_another_user_still_succeeds_and_clears_cookies).
documents.s: Logout and logout-all are idempotent about an already-dead refresh token

documents.t: Login has a generic sliding-window request limiter per source IP and a separate failed-login lockout keyed by the normalized account/source-IP pair (MAX_FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP). The pair key prevents failures against one account from consuming another account's budget behind a shared VPN/NAT exit, and prevents an attacker on one network from locking the account for users on other networks. The generic per-IP request limiter remains the aggregate cap for one source. The two serve different purposes: The rate limiter caps request volume generically (applied to all 13 decorated routes in auth_routes.py and to every route in passkey_routes.py: signup, login, OAuth2 login/callback, /auth/me, logout, logout-all, session listing/revocation, password-reset request/confirm, and account-verification request/confirm). The lockout service specifically tracks failed authentication attempts for an account/source-IP pair. A user sharing the same account and egress with an attacker can still be throttled for that pair; users attempting other accounts behind the same VPN keep independent failure budgets. See Brute-force lockout for the tradeoff and tuning settings. POST /auth/refresh/ is deliberately not rate-limited by this mechanism: the refresh flow already has its own protection via single-use token rotation and reuse detection (see above), which a generic request-volume limiter would only duplicate. See Login.
documents.s: Rate limiting and lockout are layered, not singular

documents.t: RateLimiterService.record_request (auth/security/rate_limiting/rate_limiter_service.py) catches every Valkey exception and returns False ("not allowed"). Because all 13 rate-limited routes in auth_routes.py (and the passkey routes) depend on this, a Valkey outage makes every one of them reject every caller: a full, if temporary, authentication-surface outage, not just degraded rate limiting. Most routes surface that as a JSON 429; the two OAuth2 routes (oauth2_login/oauth2_callback) redirect to /login?error=TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS instead, via rate_limited's redirect_url param, since they're top-level browser navigations with nowhere sensible to render a JSON body. This was reviewed and kept as-is, deliberately. The alternative, fail open (treat a Valkey outage as "unlimited," letting every request through unthrottled), would silently disable brute-force and credential-stuffing protection across the entire authentication surface at precisely the moment (infrastructure instability) an attacker is statistically most likely to be probing for exactly that kind of gap. A temporary full-surface 429 is recoverable and visible (users see errors, monitoring/alerting on 429 rates would catch it); a temporary silent removal of all rate limiting is neither. For a template whose purpose is an authentication foundation, fail-closed is the safer default to ship. This is a genuine availability/security tradeoff, not a free resolution either way: a deployment with different priorities (e.g. one that treats any auth downtime as worse than degraded brute-force protection, because Valkey outages are rare and monitored separately) can override it by changing record_request's except clause to return True instead. That should be a deliberate, reviewed change for that specific deployment, not this template's default.
documents.s: Rate limiter fails closed on a Valkey outage: reviewed, kept intentionally

documents.t: New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. See Security Decisions for the full index, including auth/session and product decisions. This page covers the why behind infrastructure choices: image builds, settings parsing, error monitoring, and the background task queue.

Two real, verified bugs found during a pre-release image-contents audit, both about files that exist on a developer's machine ending up baked into a Docker image that gets built and potentially shipped from that machine. Neither is something a template consumer needs to act on, since the fix is already in .dockerignore. Local access logs (backend/logs/) were baked into the backend image. backend/mystic_auth/logging/logging_config.py creates this directory on import and writes real request data to it (paths, timestamps, correlation IDs) via a TimedRotatingFileHandler. .dockerignore had *.log, which only matches paths ending in exactly .log: the rotated sibling files that handler creates (access.log.2026-07-19, not access.log.log) don't match, and backend.Dockerfile's COPY backend/ . copied them straight in. Verified concretely: a throwaway container built from the image (no bind mount) had 23MB of real local backend/logs/* content sitting in it. This isn't just wasted space: it's a snapshot of whoever's local dev traffic happened to be in that directory at build time, shipped inside a distributable artifact, and it made every image build non-reproducible (content depended on the builder's own local log history). Fixed by adding backend/logs/ explicitly. __pycache__/ and related patterns weren't actually excluding nested directories. .dockerignore had bare __pycache__/, *.pyc, *.pytest_cache/, which look like they should match at any depth, but empirically didn't: a built image still contained __pycache__/ directories nested under backend/app/**/ and backend/mystic_auth/**/ (bytecode caches that accumulate on the host filesystem because docker-compose.dev.yml's dev backend service bind-mounts ./backend:/app, so Python running inside that container writes .pyc files straight back to the host, not into an isolated container layer). Verified by building the image both before and after the fix and listing its actual contents each time. Fixed by using explicit **/-prefixed recursive patterns (**/__pycache__/, **/*.pyc, **/.pytest_cache/) instead of relying on bare patterns to recurse on their own. Not affected: the production-target frontend image (docker/mystic_auth/dockerfiles/frontend.Dockerfile's production target), verified separately, since it only ever copies --from=builder /app/dist (the compiled static bundle) into the final nginx stage, never the intermediate builder/dev stages' full source tree where a stray frontend/coverage/ (also newly excluded, though harmless content, not a leak) would have mattered. CI now has a regression guard for the backend/logs/ case specifically; see CI/CD Overview. See .dockerignore for the full current exclusion list.
documents.s: .dockerignore previously let local files leak into built images

documents.t: backend/mystic_auth/core/settings.py's Settings.Config sets extra = "ignore", overriding pydantic-settings' own default of extra = "forbid". Reason: env/mystic_auth/.env.dev isn't exclusively this app's config file. Compose env_file: directives also hand the whole file to infra-only services that have no corresponding Settings field (VALKEY_PASSWORD for valkey-server --requirepass; BUGSINK_* for the optional self-hosted error-monitoring service, see Error Monitoring). Why this was a confusing bug to track down: with the default "forbid", any such var crashed Settings() construction outright, but only sometimes. Settings.env_file = "env/mystic_auth/.env.dev" is a relative path, so it only resolves to a real file (triggering pydantic-settings' own direct file parse, which builds a dict of literally every key in the file, not just ones it recognizes) when the process's working directory is the repo root. The running app (WORKDIR /app in the Docker image) never hits this, since a relative env/mystic_auth/.env.dev there resolves to nothing and pydantic-settings falls back to reading only its declared fields from os.environ. Running the test suite with -w /repo (required so tests can import backend.app.../backend.mystic_auth..., per Testing Overview) does hit it, since /repo/env/mystic_auth/.env.dev genuinely exists there: so the exact same env/mystic_auth/.env.dev silently worked for the running app while crashing every test collection. extra = "ignore" makes both paths behave identically instead. See tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/core/test_settings_unit.py. Known trade-off, accepted deliberately: "ignore" also means a genuine typo in a variable this app does care about (SENTRY_DSNN instead of SENTRY_DSN, say) is silently dropped rather than raising a loud, easy-to-spot error: you'd only notice because the feature it configures quietly stays off, not because Settings() complained. SECRET_KEY and every other field this app treats as load-bearing are still fully validated on their own terms regardless (see _secret_key_minimum_strength below, and each field's required-vs-defaulted status in Settings itself): extra = "ignore" only affects keys the model was never going to look at anyway. Given env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example documents every real field inline, this was judged the better trade against a shared env/mystic_auth/.env.dev file crashing the app outright over a var another service in the same compose stack legitimately needs.
documents.s: Settings ignores env vars it doesn't declare, because .env is shared with Docker Compose

documents.t: error_monitoring/sentry_service.py::init_sentry() runs unguarded at import time in main.py, before the app's own global_exception_handler exists to catch anything: it has to protect itself. sentry_sdk.init() raises (sentry_sdk.utils.BadDsn) on a malformed DSN string, verified directly: sentry_sdk.init(dsn="not-a-valid-dsn-at-all", ...) throws rather than degrading gracefully. Since SENTRY_DSN is meant to be a purely optional, best-effort setting (see Error Monitoring), a typo in it must not be able to take down authentication for every user. init_sentry() now wraps the sentry_sdk.init() call in a broad try/except, logs a clear warning (via get_startup_logger(), so it's visible directly in docker compose logs rather than buried in the routine-INFO-is-file-only log: see Backend Architecture: logging), and returns with monitoring left off. The app itself starts regardless. See tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/error_monitoring/test_sentry_service_unit.py (test_init_sentry_does_not_raise_when_the_dsn_is_malformed, test_init_sentry_logs_a_warning_when_the_dsn_is_malformed). Also verified, separately: capture_exception() itself (called from the global exception handler on every request) is safe to call even when no Sentry client was ever successfully bound. sentry_sdk's own public API is designed to never raise, by the SDK's own design principle that error-reporting code must never become a worse failure than the error it was reporting. Confirmed directly rather than assumed: calling capture_exception() with no init_sentry() ever having run produces no exception. A related, separately-found bug in the same area: JWTService.create_verification_token previously hardcoded the JWT's own exp claim to ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES (15min default) regardless of what its caller requested, while account_verification_service.py set the paired Valkey single-use key's TTL (and the verification email's own wording) to RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES (60min default). A user clicking the link between 15 and 60 minutes in got a confusing invalid/expired error despite the email and the Valkey key both saying it should still work. Fixed by threading expires_minutes through from the caller. Password-reset tokens (password_service.create_reset_token) were never affected: they build their own JWT directly with the caller's expires_minutes, a separate code path. See tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/token_logic/test_jwt_service_unit.py (test_create_verification_token_honors_explicit_expires_minutes) and tests/backend/mystic_auth/unit/auth/verify_account/test_account_verification_service_unit.py (test_create_verification_token_forwards_expires_minutes_to_jwt_service).
documents.s: A malformed SENTRY_DSN must never crash the app

documents.t: The app is fully async, so the queue needs async def workers. Celery is mature and has richer workflows, but its worker model is synchronous, so async task code would need asyncio.run(...) per task, and it needs its own broker. Jobs run on Procrastinate, which is async-native and stores jobs in the Postgres database the app already trusts. (An earlier version used Taskiq on Valkey Streams.) Why Postgres instead of a Valkey broker: A permanently failed email job stays in procrastinate_jobs as status='failed', so failures are queryable and alertable. With a Valkey stream, an exhausted job was simply dropped. A retry's due time lives on the job row and the worker's own fetch query picks it up. There is no separate scheduler process whose outage could silently stop retries. Valkey stays a cache and counter store only (rate limits, lockout, token-version cache), so a flush cannot lose a queued job. What it looks like: backend/mystic_auth/procrastinate_tasks/ (procrastinate_app.py's App/PsycopgConnector, email_tasks.py, account_purge_tasks.py). One Alembic migration applies Procrastinate's packaged schema SQL, read from the installed package, so schema changes stay Alembic-only. The procrastinate_worker container runs procrastinate --app=...worker (which also runs the periodic deferrer) and uses procrastinate ... healthchecks as its healthcheck.
documents.s: Background task queue: Procrastinate on Postgres

documents.t: Every service previously connected to Postgres as the same postgres superuser (DATABASE_URL), including the request-serving backend and the Procrastinate worker's task bodies. Migration b1e6a9f3c7d2_add_least_privilege_app_role.py adds a second role, mystic_auth_app, with only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on application tables: no CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE, no CREATEROLE/CREATEDB, no superuser. database/connection.py prefers the new APP_DATABASE_URL setting when it's set, falling back to DATABASE_URL otherwise, so this is opt-in and backward-compatible; env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example ships it enabled by default for fresh setups. Migrations (alembic upgrade head) still run as the postgres superuser, since DDL and role management require it. See Database Design: Database roles for the diagram and full mechanics. Why this is worth doing even though PBAC already governs access: PBAC decides what an authenticated request is allowed to do, entirely inside the Python application. It says nothing about what Postgres itself will permit a given credential to do, independent of the application layer: a compromised dependency reusing the app's live DB connection, a bad ad hoc script, or a leaked runtime credential all bypass PBAC by construction, since PBAC never runs outside AuthorizationService.authorize(). Least-privilege role separation is standard production hygiene regardless of the app's own authorization model (every managed Postgres provider enforces it by default), and it's cheap: one role, a handful of GRANTs, no ongoing per-table maintenance. What this does and does not protect against, precisely: It does not protect the app's own data confidentiality or integrity from a leaked runtime credential: mystic_auth_app necessarily has full CRUD on application tables to function, so a leaked APP_DATABASE_URL can still read every row or overwrite them, exactly as a leaked superuser credential could. That risk needs secrets management and network-level restrictions (Postgres unreachable from outside the app's own private network), not a DB-role change, and is out of scope here. What the role split does narrow, for that same leaked credential: it can no longer run schema-destroying DDL, create a new Postgres role (e.g. a persistence backdoor), or read another role's credentials (pg_authid), capability outside the app's own table data, not inside it. Why not Row-Level Security: considered and deliberately not implemented. RLS's actual purpose is filtering which rows a role sees within a shared table, which only matters when a table holds rows belonging to multiple untrusted parties connecting with different roles: the classic case is multi-tenant SaaS, or an architecture where Postgres itself is a direct trust boundary (e.g. Supabase, where RLS is the security boundary because PostgREST exposes the database straight to end-user clients). This app is single-tenant (no tenant_id/org_id anywhere) and Postgres is never a direct trust boundary: every access is mediated by the FastAPI app, where PBAC already decides everything, including privileged operations. Without a real per-row ownership column to filter on, an RLS policy here would degenerate into USING (true) for the app role: no different from the table grant this migration already does, but with an added footgun. Every future table added by a downstream fork must be remembered and explicitly ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY'd, or it defaults to open to any role with a grant rather than protected, which is worse than not having RLS at all since it looks protected but isn't. Revisit this if a downstream fork ever adds real multi-tenancy (a tenant_id/org_id column): at that point RLS becomes the standard, correct defense-in-depth layer underneath the app's own tenant checks.
documents.s: Least-privilege app DB role instead of running as Postgres superuser

documents.t: tests/backend/conftest.py now redirects DATABASE_URL/APP_DATABASE_URL to a mystic_auth_test database on the same Postgres server, instead of the real mystic_auth database a running dev stack's own backend/procrastinate_worker containers use. See Testing Overview: Dedicated test database for the mechanics. Why: a real, reproducible incident, not a hypothetical. A dev-stack procrastinate_worker container ran for 47 minutes logging 801 ConnectorException errors, then was killed. Root cause: the historical _procrastinate_app_lifecycle fixture deleted every row from procrastinate_jobs after each test, while a worker was still processing jobs in the same database (same Postgres, whether reached via the internal postgres hostname from inside the Docker network or localhost:5433 from the host). The fixture now deletes only terminal rows and leaves todo/doing jobs for the worker to finish. A real worker picking up a test-deferred job (most commonly an audit-log write, since every protected route logs one) would sometimes lose the race: it finished processing successfully, but by the time it tried to persist status='succeeded' back onto that job's row, the test's own teardown had already deleted it out from under it. "Job was not found or not in doing/todo status" was logged, then repeated on the next job, and the next, until something (most likely WSL2's own memory manager, given OOMKilled was false in Docker's own accounting) killed the container. Why the dedicated database remains necessary even with the narrower cleanup: Scoping the teardown's DELETE to only completed jobs closes the known in-flight-job race, but the underlying problem, a test suite and a live, independently-running application sharing one database's tables, is a broader hazard than just this one symptom. The same class of collision could show up anywhere else a test's cleanup fixture deletes by a query rather than by exact ownership (e.g. _cleanup_users, _cleanup_audit_log). A dedicated database removes the shared tables entirely, which is the only fix that also protects against variants of this bug nobody has hit yet. Skipped in CI: CI already provisions its own dedicated, single-purpose mystic_auth_ci Postgres service per run (see .github/workflows/ci.yml), with no dev-stack container ever running alongside it, so there's nothing there for this redirect to protect against - detected via the CI env var, set by GitHub Actions and effectively every other CI provider by convention.
documents.s: Test suite gets its own dedicated Postgres database

documents.t: An outage of the valkey container (crash, OOM, a bad deploy of its own image) makes every login attempt fail, not just the rate-limiting/lockout checks that actually live in Valkey. This was flagged in a 2026-11-02 audit as "Valkey is a full-auth single point of failure," and is a deliberate tradeoff, not an oversight left unexamined. Why not fail-open instead: considered and rejected. Rate-limiting and login-lockout state (brute-force counters, source-scoped lockouts; see Brute-force lockout) is the entire reason Valkey sits in the login path at all. If Valkey being unreachable made the login handler skip those checks and let the request through anyway, an attacker's simplest path to defeating brute-force protection becomes making Valkey unreachable (a far easier target than Postgres: no durable data to protect, trivially resource-exhausted), not guessing passwords. That failure mode is strictly worse than the current one: a fail-open bug under load trades a temporary, visible, self-healing outage (every real user sees a 503 and retries once Valkey recovers) for a silent, permanent hole (every brute-force attempt succeeds at defeating lockout for as long as the attacker can keep Valkey down, with no outward sign anything is wrong). The same reasoning was already applied, independently, to the disk-exhaustion case (Postgres PANICs and exits rather than silently accepting unsafe writes) and the SSE concurrency cap (the cap holds under real concurrent load rather than degrading). Fail-closed under an infrastructure fault is this app's consistent posture, not something to special-case away for Valkey alone. What this does leave open, honestly: a single Valkey replica is a real availability risk for a production deployment with real uptime requirements, not a theoretical one. The accepted mitigation is operational, not code: run Valkey with persistence/replication (or a managed Valkey/Redis-compatible service) in any deployment where a login outage during a Valkey blip is unacceptable. This template's own Compose files run a single valkey container by design (see each docker-compose.*.yml's valkey service), matching its stated scope of a reference implementation, not an HA cluster - a fork taking this to production with real availability targets should add replication there, not loosen the fail-closed check in backend/mystic_auth/valkey/client.py/the login handler to compensate.
documents.s: Valkey outage fails every login closed, not just rate-limiting/lockout

documents.t: security_audit_log/authorization_audit_log keep an account's email/IP/user-agent on every historical row permanently, even after that account is deleted (self-service or admin purge). An earlier version of this template anonymized a purged account's own rows in place (audit_log_repository.anonymize_for_user/anonymize_older_than, plus a daily retention job stripping PII from any row past AUDIT_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS regardless of account status). Both are gone entirely as of a 2026-11-02 audit finding, not just disabled. Why this was reversed: account deletion is the single most predictable thing a user who just did something malicious does next, and DELETE /users/{email}/purge (no grace period, unlike self-service deletion) is the last action a compromised or malicious admin can take. Automatically anonymizing an account's audit trail as a side effect of deleting it means deleting the account was the cover-up: no review step, no way to tell an innocent deletion from one specifically timed to erase evidence. Building "and also erase my paper trail" into the most obvious thing a bad actor does next is backwards for a table whose entire purpose is making bad behavior reviewable after the fact. Why the original reasoning didn't actually hold up: the anonymization was justified as GDPR right-to-erasure compliance, but the code change does not establish whether a particular deployment must erase these records. GDPR Article 17(3)(e) limits the right to erasure only where processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise, or defence of legal claims; it is not a blanket security or fraud-prevention exception. Controllers still need a lawful basis and must limit retention to what is necessary for their purposes. This implementation retains audit identifiers indefinitely, so each deployment must assess and document its own obligations, update its privacy notice, and add an appropriate retention process where required. See Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on EUR-Lex, Article 17. What enforces this, not just application code: mystic_auth_app (the role the app actually connects as) has no UPDATE and no DELETE on either table (see b1e6a9f3c7d2_add_least_privilege_app_role.py's base grant and the three migrations that have since narrowed it: 9c3e7f1a4b8d revokes DELETE, 4b8d1f6e9c2a revokes UPDATE). Both tables are SELECT+INSERT only for the app role - genuinely append-only at the database grant level, not just by convention. A compromised dependency reusing the app's live DB connection, or a bad script run with its credentials, cannot touch a row once written, regardless of what application code does or doesn't call. Policy history and the migration marker follow the same rule (6d2a8f4c1e7b): policy_history is SELECT+INSERT only for the app role, so the record of who changed which policy stays even after the policy or the person is deleted. alembic_version is SELECT only, so the app role cannot make the database claim another schema revision. Both are checked in tests/backend/mystic_auth/security/test_least_privilege_db_role.py. What this means for a fork with real compliance requirements: if an actual erasure request requires removing PII from these tables (a regulator decision, not just "an account was deleted"), that is a deliberate, manual, out-of-band operation - a DBA/operator action against the DDL-capable DATABASE_URL role, reviewed and logged outside the app itself, never something the app's own runtime role can do automatically as a side effect of a user or admin action.
documents.s: Account deletion never anonymizes the audit trail

documents.t: New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. See Security Decisions for the full index, including auth/session and infrastructure decisions. This page covers the why behind product-level scope decisions: account lifecycle, MFA, deferred features, and known gaps.

Deleting an account defaults to reversible (soft delete: is_active=False + deleted_at set, row and all FK-referencing audit/policy rows intact) rather than immediate permanent removal. Permanent removal (purge) is a separate endpoint gated by its own, more sensitive permission (users:delete_any, granted only by system_superuser): a caller who can delete accounts day-to-day cannot, by that permission alone, irreversibly destroy one. See ../database/design.md for the full mechanics, including why session invalidation is done explicitly (revoke_all_tokens_for_user) rather than relying on the refresh endpoint to notice on its own. Self-service deletion (DELETE /users/me, user_self_service_routes.py::delete_my_account) reuses this same soft-delete path, never purge: The row is soft-deleted and sessions are revoked exactly like delete_any_user, minus the path-parameterized target and the "not your own account" guard, which doesn't apply here since acting on your own account is the entire point. It writes a distinct audit event (account_deleted_self, versus permission-protected account_deleted) so the security audit log can tell the two apart at a glance. A soft-deleted account (self- or permission-protected) is not held forever: a daily Procrastinate periodic task (procrastinate_tasks/account_purge_tasks.py::purge_expired_soft_deleted_accounts, @app.periodic(cron="0 3 * * *"), running inside the worker process itself via Procrastinate's own PeriodicDeferrer, so there's no separate scheduler process for this to depend on) hard-purges any account whose deleted_at is older than ACCOUNT_PURGE_GRACE_DAYS (default 30), going through the exact same revoke → audit → delete sequence as a manual purge (user_lifecycle/user_purge_service.py::purge_user_account, shared by both call sites) so the grace-period purge and a permission-protected manual purge can never drift apart. The purged account's prior security_audit_log/authorization_audit_log rows are left exactly as written, not anonymized: see decisions-infra.md's "Account deletion never anonymizes the audit trail" for why. This is what gives self-service deletion an actual recovery window instead of either purging synchronously (no recovery at all) or never purging (an unbounded pile of soft-deleted rows). Both the soft-delete step and the actual re-authentication proving intent differ by account type, though, and deliberately so: An account with a password re-authenticates and is deleted synchronously, in the same request: The caller supplies their current password (the same password_service.verify_password call the self-service password-change flow uses). On success, delete_my_account runs the soft-delete → revoke-sessions → audit sequence immediately. It then clears the access_token/refresh_token cookies on its Response before returning (the same cookie shape logout_handler.py uses, including refresh_token's path="/auth"), a gap the endpoint had before this cookie-clearing was added, unlike every other session-ending endpoint. An OAuth-only account (hashed_password is None) has no password to re-confirm with, so an active session cookie alone would otherwise be sufficient proof: a stolen access-token cookie (e.g. via XSS) could delete the account outright with nothing else required. Rather than skip re-authentication for this case, account_deletion_service.py gives it an async, email-confirmed equivalent, modeled directly on auth/password_logic/password_reset_service.py: A signed JWT (type claim "account_delete", scoping it away from access/refresh/reset tokens sharing the same SECRET_KEY) is minted, persisted in Valkey under account_delete:{token} with a TTL from ACCOUNT_DELETE_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES (default 60), and emailed as a link to the frontend's /confirm-delete page. delete_my_account returns immediately in this branch without deleting anything: the account and the calling session stay untouched until the link is used. POST /users/me/confirm-delete (deliberately unauthenticated, same trust model as POST /auth/password-reset/confirm: the token itself is the proof, and the link must work from whatever device the caller opened their email on) redeems the token via Valkey GETDEL (atomic single-use, for the same replay-race reason password_reset_service.reset_password's doc-comment explains), then runs the exact same soft-delete → revoke-sessions → audit sequence as the password-account path. Both paths call one shared function (user_lifecycle/user_self_deletion_service.py::finalize_self_deletion) so they can't drift apart, mirroring purge_user_account's share between the permission-protected purge route and the scheduled grace-period job. The confirm endpoint also gets its own login-lockout-style rate limiting via login_protection_service.check_and_record_action, under a account_delete_confirm_lock:email: namespace distinct from both login_lock:account_ip: and password_reset_confirm_lock:email:, for the same reason those two stay distinct from each other: a stale or reused deletion link must never count towards, or be able to trip, an unrelated lockout for that email.
documents.s: Account lifecycle: soft delete by default

documents.t: No multi-factor authentication (TOTP, SMS, or a WebAuthn second factor) is implemented. This is an intentionally deferred scope boundary, not an oversight discovered late. Passkeys do exist (see Passkeys), but as an optional single-step sign-in method and as the "confirm it's you" check before changing passkeys, not as a second factor after a password. A passkey login does not populate security_context, and a password login is never made to ask for one. Why: MFA adds real user friction (a context switch to a separate device or app to retrieve a code) that isn't justified for most applications built from this template. This was a deliberate product judgment call for a template meant to stay lean, not a technical limitation. What I offer instead: optional passkeys. They resist phishing and password reuse, which is most of what a second factor is for, without a second step on every login. The same reasoning is behind the password rule (8 or more characters with upper, lower and digit, no breach check): longer minimums are hard to remember and add daily friction for little real benefit. Both choices are mine, reconfirmed on 2026-11-03, and both are marked as accepted gaps in the ASVS mapping. authorization/conditions/condition_types/security_context_condition.py and authorization/context/request_context_builder.py both carry explicit comments that security_context starts empty because this app does not implement MFA/device-trust infrastructure; any policy condition keyed on it (e.g. a hypothetical mfa_verified check) would currently always evaluate to false/deny. The PBAC condition framework (context_attributes, security_context condition types: see ../authorization/condition-schema-reference.md) was deliberately built generic enough that a real MFA layer could plug in later by populating security_context at authentication time and writing policies that key off it, without any redesign of the authorization engine itself. The mfa_verified key appears in tests and docs today purely as an illustrative example of the generic mechanism, not a real, enforced check. Any real deployment that needs MFA should treat it as a deliberate follow-up: add a TOTP enrollment+verification flow (or reuse the passkey ceremony as a second factor), populate security_context.mfa_verified on successful step-up auth, and gate sensitive policies on that context key. The hooks already exist to receive it.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. Consolidates the concrete hardening mechanisms in the codebase: rate limiting, lockout, response headers, CORS, and cookie flags. For the why behind non-obvious choices, see Security Decisions. Split by category into three pages, indexed below.

See Security Hardening: Abuse Prevention for the full entries. Rate limiting: generic per-IP/per-account limiter, fails closed on Valkey error, the Rate Limit Dashboard. Brute-force lockout: source-IP failed-login lockout, layered on top of rate limiting. Timing-attack resistance: dummy-hash comparison, unconditional hashing, identical generic responses.

See Security Hardening: HTTP Layer for the full entries. Security response headers: X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, CSP, HSTS, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy. CORS: allowed origins, credentials, methods, headers. Cookies: access_token/refresh_token/oauth_state paths and flags. Middleware ordering: why CorrelationIdMiddleware ends up outermost. Error handling: the global exception handler and AppError's structured error responses.

See Security Hardening: Infrastructure for the full entries. Valkey authentication: VALKEY_PASSWORD, embedded in VALKEY_URL. SECRET_KEY strength enforcement: rejects weak keys under 32 characters at import time. Reverse-proxy IP trust: TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS gates X-Forwarded-For trust. Session geolocation: MaxMind GeoLite2-City, off by default. Known accepted gaps: see Concerns for the current open list.

ASVS Level 3 mapping: a self-assessment against OWASP ASVS 4.0.3, with evidence per requirement and the open gaps. Threat model: assets, actors, trust boundaries and the control behind each STRIDE threat.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. Rate limiting, brute-force lockout, and timing-attack resistance: the mechanisms that push back on high-volume or automated abuse at the request layer. See Security Hardening for the full index, and Security Decisions for the why behind non-obvious choices here.

backend/mystic_auth/auth/security/rate_limiting/rate_limiter_service.py: a generic sliding-window-by-fixed-bucket limiter backed by Valkey (INCR + EXPIRE on first request in a window). Applied via the @rate_limiter_service.rate_limited("endpoint_name", account_key_func=...) decorator on every route in auth_routes.py and passkey_routes.py (passkey sign-in, management, step-up): signup, login, OAuth2 initiate/callback, /auth/me, logout, logout-all, password-reset request/confirm, verify-account request/confirm, list/revoke sessions. Not applied to refresh_token_routes.py (POST /auth/refresh/). That route relies instead on its own single-use-token rotation and reuse-detection protection (see Security Decisions), which a generic request-volume limiter would only duplicate. Always applies a per-IP limit ({endpoint_name}:ip:{ip}), resolved via auth/security/client_ip.py (trusted-proxy-aware). The two OAuth2 routes redirect instead of returning the JSON 429 shown as R429 above: oauth2_login/oauth2_callback pass rate_limited(..., redirect_url=...), so an exceeded limit sends the browser to /login?error=TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS instead - both routes are top-level navigations (they always return a RedirectResponse), not API calls with anywhere to render a JSON body. See Google OAuth2 / PKCE. Optionally applies a per-account limit when account_key_func is given (e.g. signup/password-reset-request key on the submitted email): closes the gap where an attacker spreads requests targeting one account across many source IPs to stay under the per-IP threshold alone. Both limits default to MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW / REQUEST_WINDOW_SECONDS (env/mystic_auth/.env.dev.example). Any route can override just its own threshold instead by passing rate_limited("endpoint_name", max_requests=..., window_seconds=...) - give both together (either alone still falls back to the global default for the other). A consuming project can tighten a rarely-hit, sensitive route (e.g. password-reset-request) without touching the shared default every other endpoint keeps using, and GET /auth/me (get_current_user) does the opposite: it raises its own limit to 300/60s instead of tightening. The shared 100/60s default is sized for /auth/login's brute-force risk, but /auth/me is read-only and already session-cookie-gated, and is the highest-frequency authenticated route in the app (the SPA calls it on every route mount). Measured live: a full local run of the 32-account permission-matrix e2e suite tripped the default limit on this endpoint 492 times in one run, misread for months as a WebKit/Firefox cookie-commit timing race, since a rate-limited poll and a genuinely-not-authenticated-yet poll fail with the same symptom. A real user with a few tabs open and normal navigation could plausibly trip the same default. An endpoint that overrides is recorded in RateLimiterService.ENDPOINT_OVERRIDES so the dashboard below reports the threshold it actually enforces, not the global one. Fails closed on Valkey error, reviewed and kept intentionally: record_request catches all exceptions, logs them, and returns False ("not allowed"): a Valkey outage makes every rate-limited request appear over-limit and get rejected with 429, rather than silently disabling rate limiting. This is the opposite tradeoff from the PBAC authorization cache, which fails open to the authoritative database on a Valkey error: see PBAC Troubleshooting: Valkey cache management for that contrast. Practical implication: a Valkey outage makes the API fully unusable for any rate-limited auth route, not just slower. See Security Decisions for why this was kept rather than changed. reset_counter only ever deletes an actual rate-limit key: DELETE /rate-limits/{key} (see API Reference) takes the key straight from the URL, but this same Valkey instance also holds unrelated security-critical keys (legacy revoked:{jti} markers, password-reset/verify/account-delete tokens, the PBAC policy cache, and more; current replay claims are in Postgres). reset_counter rejects any key that doesn't match the <endpoint>:<ip|account|email|account_ip>:<identifier> shape list_active_limits itself produces, so this endpoint can never be used to delete something outside the rate-limiter's own keyspace.

RateLimitDashboardService.list_active_limits powers the permission-protected dashboard, and it doesn't only read RateLimiterService.record_request's keys: it SCANs the whole <endpoint>:<ip|account|email|account_ip>:<identifier> keyspace, which also picks up Brute-force lockout's login_lock:* keys below (endpoint shows as login_lock for those rows, and _effective_limit reports their MAX_FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP threshold instead of MAX_REQUESTS_PER_WINDOW; an endpoint with its own rate_limited(..., max_requests=...) override gets its row's limit reported from RateLimiterService.ENDPOINT_OVERRIDES the same way). So one dashboard, filterable by scope (ip/account/email/account_ip), covers both mechanisms: An ip-scoped row's identifier is always an IP address. This includes generic per-endpoint request limits such as signup:ip:1.2.3.4. An account- or email-scoped row is keyed by an account identifier. The account_ip scope is the login failure counter: its identifier is an HMAC digest over the normalized email and source IP, so neither value is exposed in Valkey keys or dashboard rows. It remains resettable from the dashboard. To identify which account and IP were behind a lockout, cross-reference its login_ip_locked audit event. The durable Audit Log records the attempted email and source IP; the rate-limit key stores neither in clear text. The matched-key listing is snapshotted for _SCAN_SNAPSHOT_TTL_SECONDS (5s) per filter pattern (RateLimitDashboardService._scan_snapshot_cache, an in-process dict, not Valkey), so that paging through one filtered view walks a consistent set of keys instead of two consecutive SCANs disagreeing as counters expire/get created between page requests. reset_counter clears this entire snapshot cache on every successful delete, so a caller resetting a counter and immediately re-filtering the dashboard sees the key gone right away, rather than it lingering in the listing (with a correct, live-read count/TTL) for up to 5s until the snapshot naturally expires.

backend/mystic_auth/auth/security/login_protection_service.py: separate from and layered on top of the generic rate limiter (see Security Decisions: rate limiting and lockout are layered): Failed-login lockout is keyed by the normalized account/source-IP pair. MAX_FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP failures within LOGIN_LOCKOUT_TIME_PER_IP seconds lock only that pair (login_lock:account_ip:{HMAC(email, client_ip)}). There is no account-wide failed-attempt counter, so an attacker cannot lock the account for users coming from other IPs. People behind the same VPN/NAT egress have separate failure budgets for different accounts; an attacker using that same egress can still temporarily throttle the same account/IP pair. The generic per-IP request limiter is the aggregate cap across accounts. check_and_record_action's failure path is a single atomic Valkey INCR, not a separate is_locked-then-record pair. A check-then-increment version would let concurrent failures against the same key both read "not yet locked" before either incremented, letting more than max_attempts through as 401 under a real burst; the atomic INCR closes that race (test_login_lockout_race_integration.py). The pair counter uses INCR/EXPIRE-on-first-failure (not sliding), so the lockout window is fixed from the first failure, not extended by each subsequent one. The env setting names retain _PER_IP for compatibility, but their threshold and expiry apply to the account/IP pair. Passkey sign-in failures lock per source IP (login_lock:ip:{HMAC("passkey", client_ip)}) and failed step-up confirmations per account and IP (login_lock:account_ip:{HMAC("stepup", email, client_ip)}), both using the _PER_IP settings, so they show up in the dashboard like password lockouts. See Passkeys. The active key is visible and resettable from the Rate Limit Dashboard above, under endpoint login_lock - there's no separate lockout-specific view. The 429 a lockout returns tells the caller how long to actually wait, read straight from the tripped key's remaining Valkey TTL (get_remaining_seconds): a standard Retry-After header (RFC 9110) plus params.minutes (rounded up) in the JSON body for the login form's own translated message. See Login for the full response shape.

The rate limiter and lockout counters are ephemeral (Valkey TTL-expired). The login account_ip key stores only an HMAC digest, not raw email or IP. For a durable, per-event history that does include ip_address (e.g. "which IPs hit this account's failed logins"), use the Audit Log instead: backend/mystic_auth/audit_log/, GET /audit/security-log, filterable by ip_address (see API Reference). It's a separate Postgres-backed record of individual events, not a live counter.

The lockout above counts failures per account and source IP, so guessing spread over many addresses never trips it. A second counter (auth/security/account_cooldown_service.py) counts failed logins for one account from every source. After LOGIN_ACCOUNT_FAILURE_THRESHOLD (20) failures inside LOGIN_ACCOUNT_FAILURE_WINDOW_SECONDS (15 minutes) the account is in a cool-down: it accepts one login attempt per LOGIN_ACCOUNT_COOLDOWN_SECONDS (30), and other attempts get 429 with Retry-After. It is a cool-down, not a lock, on purpose. A hard lock would let anyone shut the real owner out by guessing wrong passwords on purpose. With a cool-down the attacker is held to about two guesses a minute, while the owner signs in after at most 30 seconds, and a successful sign-in clears the count. Crossing the threshold writes a login_account_cooldown audit event and sends one alert. Failed attempts are counted by the submitted email whether or not the account exists, so the behaviour reveals nothing about which accounts exist. IPv6: all per-source counters (rate limits, login lockouts, refresh lockouts) group an IPv6 address by its /64 prefix, because one customer normally controls the whole /64 and could otherwise rotate through addresses without ever reaching a limit. In the Rate Limits page such a row shows as v6-2001-0db8-aaaa-bbbb.

Passwords are NFKC-normalized (NIST SP 800-63B) before they are hashed or checked, in password_service.normalize_password. The same typed password then works however a device composes accented or full-width characters, for example "é" as one character or as "e" plus a combining accent. Hashes made before this change were computed on the text exactly as typed, so a normalization-changed input is also checked against the raw form. Ordinary ASCII passwords still cost one Argon2 check.
See Security Decisions: timing-attack mitigations: applied at login (dummy-hash comparison), signup (unconditional hashing), and password-reset-request (identical generic response).

Key names show up in SCAN, dumps, backups and monitoring tools, so no account email appears in one. Rate-limit account counters, lockout counters, the authorization cache and the session-event channels use email_key_id(email) (backend/mystic_auth/valkey/key_names.py), an HMAC of the lower-cased address under SECRET_KEY. Emailed one-time tokens (verify, account deletion) are keyed by their SHA-256. The stored key stays hashed, but the Rate Limits page still shows who a counter belongs to: the server recomputes the id for known accounts (and, for account_ip lockout counters, for the email and IP of failed attempts in the last 24 hours of the security audit log) and returns the match as identifier_label in the response only (auth/security/rate_limiting/rate_limit_identifier_labels.py). A counter that matches nobody shows a shortened id with the full value on hover. Anyone with rate_limits:read therefore sees the emails of accounts that have live counters, as they did before the ids were hashed. Searching the identifier filter with a full address still finds an account counter, but not an account_ip one, which also needs the source IP. Rotating SECRET_KEY changes every id, which only resets these short-lived counters and caches.
documents.s: No email addresses in Valkey key names

documents.t: Every sign-in, sign-up and password change runs Argon2, which costs about 0.4 CPU-seconds. A container with 2 CPUs therefore sustains only about 4 to 5 of them per second, however they arrive. Without a bound, a burst queues behind that limit and callers wait until their client gives up (30 seconds in the load test). Each worker now runs at most PASSWORD_HASH_CONCURRENCY hashes at once (default 1) and lets at most PASSWORD_HASH_MAX_WAITING more wait (default 2). Anyone beyond that gets 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE with Retry-After: 5 straight away, the same answer used for a store outage. The refused request is not counted as a failed sign-in, a sign-up is not reported as successful, and a password-reset link that was consumed is put back. The rest of the API stays responsive while this happens. Measured on the 2-CPU local stack with 200 sign-in attempts across fresh accounts at 60 at a time: before the bound, the slowest request took 28 seconds; after, 6 seconds, with the excess refused. Capacity is unchanged, because the CPU cost per hash is the same. To serve more sign-ins per second, give the backend more CPUs.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. Response headers, CORS, cookie flags, middleware ordering, and error handling: the mechanisms that shape what the HTTP layer itself exposes to a client. See Security Hardening for the full index.

backend/mystic_auth/middleware/security_headers_middleware.py, applied to every response: Header Value Reasoning X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Stops MIME-type sniffing X-Frame-Options DENY This is a JSON API with no HTML pages of its own beyond the auto-generated docs below: no framing use case exists Content-Security-Policy default-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none' on every route except /docs//redoc//openapi.json (see below) Zero functional cost on the real API surface since there's no HTML/script to allow Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains (production only: see below) Forces HTTPS for a year, protecting the cookies from protocol downgrade Referrer-Policy no-referrer URLs here can carry sensitive query params (OAuth2 state/code) Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=() This is a JSON API with no page of its own that would ever invoke these browser features: denying them closes off a class of clickjacking-adjacent abuse at zero functional cost Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin No legitimate cross-origin window needs to reference this one Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy same-origin Blocks cross-origin scripts from reading these responses (Spectre-style side channels) Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy require-corp (skipped on /docs and the other doc paths, since jsdelivr/Google Fonts don't opt in via CORP/CORS) Same rationale as COOP/CORP above HSTS is gated on settings.ENVIRONMENT == "production" (checked fresh per request, not cached at import time). Sending it unconditionally would pin HSTS for a full year against real browser traffic even in a non-production deployment served over plain HTTP, with no way to turn it off short of a code change: browsers ignore the header over plain HTTP today, but that's not a reason to send a year-long pin somewhere it isn't intended to apply yet. /docs, /redoc, and /openapi.json get a relaxed CSP, carved out by request path. FastAPI's auto-generated Swagger UI (/docs) and ReDoc (/redoc) pages are enabled whenever ENVIRONMENT != "production" (see backend/app/main.py), and are the one place this API actually serves HTML. Both load their JS/CSS from a CDN (cdn.jsdelivr.net) plus an inline <script>/<style> block; ReDoc additionally pulls a Google Fonts stylesheet. A blanket default-src 'none' policy here would not error or warn: the page would return 200 and render silently blank, every asset blocked with nothing in the response to say why. security_headers_middleware.py's _DOCS_PATHS/_DOCS_CSP scope a permissive-but-specific policy (cdn.jsdelivr.net, fonts.googleapis.com/fonts.gstatic.com, 'unsafe-inline') to exactly those three paths; every other route keeps the strict policy above. Strict-Transport-Security on the frontend static build is set by nginx itself (docker/mystic_auth/nginx.frontend.conf), unconditionally rather than gated on ENVIRONMENT like the backend's copy: the frontend production image only ever ships in a production-shaped deployment, and needs to send it itself since the local-prod-ngrok/cloudflare/tailscale tunnel modes have no other layer in front of it that would. docker/mystic_auth/Caddyfile (the real prod TLS terminator) deliberately does not also set it: nginx already covers every response reaching Caddy, backend and frontend alike, so Caddy adding it too would just duplicate the header. See Docker Overview. docker/mystic_auth/nginx.frontend.conf mirrors most of the backend's header set for the SPA response (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, plus its own less-strict CSP), and also disables server_tokens to stop the nginx version leaking in the Server response header. The frontend's style-src, style-src-elem and script-src have no 'unsafe-inline', and there is no style-src-attr allowance. Two Radix internals (the scroll lock behind every dialog/menu/popover, and the Select viewport) inject a <style> element at runtime whose content cannot be hashed ahead of time. nginx therefore stamps a fresh random nonce ($request_id) into the <meta name="csp-nonce"> of every SPA response and allows exactly that nonce in style-src-elem; frontend/src/mystic_auth/core/cspNonce.ts publishes it as __webpack_nonce__ and the Select viewports receive it as a prop. SPA responses are no-store so a nonce is never reused. React applies style={...} through the CSSOM, which CSP does not restrict, so inline style attributes need no allowance (a sweep of every route under the enforced policy found zero violations). ci/mystic_auth/frontend-csp-nonce-smoke.py checks the nonce wiring against the built image. If you add a library that injects <style> tags, give it the nonce rather than loosening the policy. Earlier notes on the hash-only parts follow. The one style-src hash and the one script-src hash are both confirmed against the current build: they cover frontend/index.html's pre-React boot shell, a <style> block for its layout/colors and a small synchronous <script> that sets its dark/light mode from localStorage before paint. Confirmed live by removing every other hash and sweeping every route (all authenticated and public pages, all 7 language modes, including the dashboard chart's hover tooltip) with a securitypolicyviolation listener armed: zero violations, so nothing else in the current build needs an inline-style/script allowance. A real CSP violation on exactly this boot-shell <style> block was found and fixed live in an earlier pass (the browser silently drops a disallowed inline style or script, so the failure mode is a rendering bug, not a console error a casual check would catch) - do not assume "the page rendered fine" during any check meant the CSP was actually satisfied; check the browser console for securitypolicyviolation/CSP messages directly. A separate, unrelated violation was later found and fixed the same way: three of the app's own components injected runtime <style> tags via React's <style href precedence> resource-hoisting API, which a hash-only CSP can never allow since their content has no fixed hash to add ahead of time - moved into the app stylesheet (theme/application.css) instead, the only fix that works under this CSP. See the comment above style-src/script-src in docker/mystic_auth/nginx.frontend.conf for exactly what each hash covers and how to regenerate it. The shared frontend toast renderer (frontend/src/mystic_auth/ui/toaster/) is template-owned and styled from the bundled Tailwind stylesheet. It deliberately does not use a library that injects runtime <style> tags, so toast notifications remain compatible with the strict production CSP without adding 'unsafe-inline'. Downstream projects should use the exposed toaster/components from frontend/src/app/sdk.ts; changes to shared toast styling belong in an upstream contribution, not in frontend/src/mystic_auth/theme/application.css. nginx parser-level errors carry the security headers. 414 (request line too long) and 431 (header too large) are raised while nginx is still parsing the request, before any location is matched. error_page therefore points at URI-based internal locations (/_security_error/<code>), not @named ones: a named-location redirect fails at that stage with empty URI in redirect and a bare 500. Header-too-large is nginx's internal code 494, which is mapped to 431 explicitly (otherwise it is sent as a bare 400). Verified against the pinned nginx build with a 9000-byte URI and a 9000-byte header; re-verify both when bumping the nginx image.

backend/app/main.py: CORSMiddleware is configured as follows. Allowed origins: settings.cors_allowed_origins (FRONTEND_BASE_URL plus any comma-separated FRONTEND_ADDITIONAL_BASE_URLS; single-origin by default). Credentials: allow_credentials=True, required for cookie-based auth to work cross-origin in dev, where frontend :5173 and backend :8000 are different origins. Methods: restricted to GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Headers: restricted to Content-Type. Redirect/email links (OAuth callback, verification, password reset) always point at FRONTEND_BASE_URL alone regardless of how many origins are CORS-allowed: there's always exactly one canonical link target.

Cookie Path Flags Set by access_token / httponly, secure outside development, samesite=Strict token_cookie_handler.py refresh_token /auth httponly, secure outside development, samesite=Strict token_cookie_handler.py oauth_state / httponly, secure outside development, samesite=Lax (must survive Google's cross-site redirect) oauth2_login_handler.py The development stack uses plain HTTP, so it intentionally omits Secure for browser compatibility. Local-prod and production must use HTTPS and set Secure; the setting is derived from ENVIRONMENT, not from a request-controlled host or scheme.

SameSite=Strict cookies and the CORS allow-list stop cross-site forgery, but a same-site sibling (another subdomain under the same registrable domain) is still allowed to send cookies. OriginCheckMiddleware (middleware/origin_check_middleware.py) closes that gap for POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE: A request whose Origin is a configured frontend origin, or has the same hostname as the request's own Host, is accepted. Any other Origin (including null) gets 403 CROSS_ORIGIN_REQUEST_BLOCKED. A request with no Origin is accepted unless Sec-Fetch-Site says a browser sent it cross-site, so curl, server-to-server calls and tests keep working. It is plain ASGI, not BaseHTTPMiddleware, so it does not touch streaming responses.

main.py adds middleware in this order: CORSMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware, SecurityHeadersMiddleware, then CorrelationIdMiddleware last. Starlette applies middleware in reverse of add order, so CorrelationIdMiddleware ends up outermost. This ensures request.state.request_id (and the logging contextvar it sets) is populated before any other middleware or route logic runs.

Two handlers registered in main.py: Global @app.exception_handler(Exception): catches every otherwise-unhandled exception, logs it with a full traceback, and returns a generic 500 {"detail": "Internal Server Error"}. Internal exception details never reach the client, regardless of ENVIRONMENT; debug= is never passed to the FastAPI app either (defaults False), so there's no path where Starlette's own debug error page could leak a traceback. This same handler also reports the exception for error monitoring (error_monitoring.sentry_service.capture_exception): a no-op unless SENTRY_DSN is set. See Error Monitoring. More specific @app.exception_handler(AppError): catches core/errors.py's AppError, the structured exception routes raise on purpose (AppError(status_code, code, detail, params=None)), and returns {"detail", "code", "params"} instead of the generic body above. code is a stable, machine-readable identifier (e.g. "INVALID_CREDENTIALS"). The frontend's api/apiError.ts looks it up in errors.json to render a translated message, falling back to the English detail for any route not yet migrated to AppError. See API Reference: error responses and Translations Overview.

The frontend nginx falls back to index.html for client-side routes, but not for static-looking paths. A missing file under /assets/, /robots.txt or /.well-known/ returns a real 404 (through the security-header error location) instead of the SPA page with status 200. To publish a robots.txt or security.txt, put the file in the frontend's public/ folder and it is served with the usual security headers.

New to a term here? See the Infrastructure Glossary or Authentication Glossary. Valkey authentication, secret strength, reverse-proxy IP trust, session geolocation, and the current accepted-gaps list. See Security Hardening for the full index.

VALKEY_PASSWORD is required by every production and local-production Compose mode and is passed to valkey-server --requirepass; the Compose files fail before startup if it is missing. The development mode defaults email off but still receives a generated Valkey password from setup-env. Since valkey-py (valkey/client.py) authenticates through the connection URL rather than a separate kwarg, the same password is embedded in VALKEY_URL (redis://:<VALKEY_PASSWORD>@valkey:6379/0) by setup-env. (Background jobs no longer use Valkey at all: procrastinate_tasks/ runs on the same Postgres instance as everything else, see Background Email Delivery.)

core/settings.py rejects any SECRET_KEY under 32 characters at import time (Settings._secret_key_minimum_strength): a placeholder/example value fails fast at startup instead of silently signing tokens with weak entropy. This is a length floor, not a real entropy check (a 32-character low-entropy string still passes).

auth/security/client_ip.py::get_client_ip only trusts X-Forwarded-For when the literal TCP peer is listed in TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS (empty/untrusted by default): every rate-limit, lockout, audit-log, and PBAC context call site goes through it (rate_limited refuses, at import time, a handler that has no request parameter, so none can fall into a shared bucket). IPv6 addresses are grouped by their /64 prefix (ip_bucket) for per-source counters. Deploying behind a reverse proxy only requires setting TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS to that proxy's address, no code change needed. In the prod/local-prod-* Compose files, that value is derived automatically from FRONTEND_STATIC_IP/the tunnel's *_STATIC_IP var (see Routing: Trusted proxy IPs) rather than set directly in .env. Settings.TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS defaults to "" so it doesn't need to be present in the env file at all: only the backend service gets the derived value (via that Compose environment: override); alembic and procrastinate_worker read the same env file directly, never use this setting, and fall back to the default instead of failing to start.

Resolves each login's city/country from its IP via a local MaxMind GeoLite2-City database, off by default. Split out into its own doc since it has a full setup flow (MaxMind account, license key, Docker profile) rather than being a simple config flag: see Session Geolocation.

See Concerns for the current open list (non-blocking performance tests, horizontal scaling). pytest does not ship in the production backend image: docker/mystic_auth/dockerfiles/backend.Dockerfile's multi-stage build has a runtime target (no test tooling, the default and the only target backend/procrastinate_worker/alembic actually run) and a separate test target that layers requirements-dev.txt on top of it, selected via the backend service's target: ${BACKEND_BUILD_TARGET:-runtime} in docker-compose.dev.yml. Error monitoring is available: see Error Monitoring.

Product-specific credentials belong to the downstream application. MysticAuth provides a small secret-provider contract; it does not store integration credentials in its database or configuration model.

Implement SecretProvider in backend/app/ and register your provider from the downstream startup hook in backend/app/app_sdk.py. Import the public contract from app.sdk: from app.sdk import SecretProvider, require_secret class BillingSecrets: def __init__(self, provider: SecretProvider) -> None: self._provider = provider def api_key(self) -> str: return require_secret(self._provider, "BILLING_API_KEY") SecretProvider.get_secret(name) reads one named value and returns None when the value is absent. require_secret(provider, name) raises a clear configuration error if the value is missing or empty. The built-in EnvironmentSecretProvider reads only the requested variable from the process environment and rejects names that are not valid environment identifiers.

For local development, provide values through the ignored app runtime env file (env/app/.env.dev) or your local secret manager. For deployment, inject them through the host's secret manager or the app-specific Compose configuration. Keep secret values out of tracked .example files; examples should document variable names and safe placeholders only. Keep product settings in backend/app/core/settings.py and app-specific env templates under env/app/. Read a secret at the point the integration needs it. Do not dump the full environment or secret mapping into logs, API responses, task arguments, migrations, audit metadata, or JSON settings. Tests should inject a small fake provider rather than relying on a developer's real credentials.

Provider implementations, integration clients, their settings, and tests belong under backend/app/ and tests/backend/app/. Do not add product credentials or product-specific providers under backend/mystic_auth/; that tree is upstream-owned. See The app/ + mystic_auth/ Split and Building On This Template.

New to a term here? See the Authentication Glossary or Infrastructure Glossary. A short threat model for MysticAuth: what it protects, who might attack it, where the trust boundaries are, and which control answers each threat. It uses the STRIDE categories (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege). Review it whenever a new sign-in method, a new data store, or a new public route is added. This is a design-level document written from the code and docs. It is not a penetration test result. Controls named here link to the page that explains them.

Asset Why it matters Password hashes (Argon2id) Offline cracking if the database leaks Sessions and tokens (access, refresh) Taking one is taking the account Passkey public keys and credential ids Low value alone, but they decide who can sign in Policies and permission grants Changing them changes who can do what The security audit log The evidence trail after an incident Email, name and profile data Personal data, plus the verification and reset channel Secrets (SECRET_KEY, database passwords, backup key, OAuth client secret) Forging tokens, reading or restoring data Backups A full copy of everything above

Actor Can do Cannot do Anonymous internet user Hit public routes, guess passwords, try signup and reset flows, send crafted input Reach Postgres or Valkey directly Authenticated ordinary user Use their own account, try to reach other accounts or higher permissions Grant themselves permissions they do not hold Holder of a narrow permission (for example policies:create) Use that permission Mint or assign anything they do not already hold Attacker with a stolen session or refresh token Act as the user until it is revoked Re-use a rotated refresh token without it being detected Phisher Trick a user into typing a password Use a passkey on a fake site Compromised dependency Run code inside the backend or frontend Be assumed away: this is why CI scans dependencies Operator mistake Misconfigure CORS, proxies, secrets Be fully prevented; checks exist but a human still deploys Out of scope: an attacker with root on the host, a compromised database superuser, and a compromised identity provider (Google).
Everything from the browser is untrusted, including cookies, headers, the Origin, and any client-side check. The frontend only hides what the user may not do. The backend decides.

Threat Control Password guessing and credential stuffing Per-IP and per-account rate limits, source-scoped lockout, Argon2id, see Abuse prevention Learning which emails are registered Generic responses, signup always returns the same body, dummy-hash timing, see Timing-attack resistance Stolen session cookie HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict, short access token, rotating single-use refresh token with reuse detection, per-session revoke and sign out everywhere Phishing Optional passkeys are bound to the site, so a fake site cannot use them Forged tokens Signed JWTs with pinned algorithm, issuer and audience, SECRET_KEY strength enforced at start-up Fake OAuth callback oauth_state cookie and PKCE, see OAuth2 PKCE Spoofed client IP X-Forwarded-For trusted only from TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS, see Reverse-proxy IP trust

Threat Control SQL injection SQLAlchemy parameterised queries, Pydantic schemas on every route Cross-site request forgery SameSite=Strict cookies, restricted CORS to the configured origins, JSON-only bodies Editing the audit trail The application database role has UPDATE and DELETE on the audit log revoked Tampering with a backup Detached HMAC-SHA256 tag checked before restore, see Database backup A caller widening their own permissions assert_authorized_to_grant blocks granting anything the caller does not hold, with mutation-checked tests Replaying a one-time link Verification, reset and deletion tokens are single use and expire

Threat Control "I never did that" Security audit log for sign-in, logout, passkey, role, policy and lifecycle events, with IP, user agent and request id Operator actions on another account Audited with the acting user, for example removed_by on operator passkey removal Silent credential changes The account holder is emailed when a passkey is added or removed
